### `drift-guard-test-hook-hygiene`: serialize the drift-guard test helper's panic-hook swap (R3-CQ-1 residual)

The `precondition_rejects` test helper in `src/agents_md_drift.rs` swaps the process-global panic hook (take a no-op hook, run `catch_unwind`, restore) without serialization. Under parallel `cargo test`, two callers' take/set pairs can interleave and transiently leave the no-op hook installed, suppressing a concurrent or subsequent real panic's backtrace.

Ruled VALID but NON-BLOCKING (low) in the `agents-md-drift-guard` round-3 triage and accepted as a residual: it is diagnostic-only (each call captures its result via `catch_unwind(...).is_err()`, independent of the hook), so it cannot flip any test's pass/fail and is not a flake; the only impact is backtrace visibility under a parallel failure.

Fix options: serialize the swap behind a `Mutex`, drop the hook swap entirely, or set the no-op hook once for the test binary. Deferred; low priority.

### `code-value-audit-static`: the cheap static-only code-value report (`Q-52`)

Build the Tier-0 slice of the Q-52 code-value audit: an advisory report of code that may not be earning its keep, computed from ZERO/low-cost STATIC signals only, projected from a machine-readable intermediate (JSON) to a kept `docs/plans/<task>.code-value-report.md` (Structured data first, project for humans). Signals: rustc `dead_code` / `unused_*` warnings harvested from `cargo build --message-format=json` (free); `#[allow(dead_code)]` / `#[expect(dead_code)]` markers read as author-declared reasons, NOT candidates (Chesterton's Fence encoded in the source, e.g. `Check::budget` / `Check::threshold` at `src/checks.rs:135`, `src/checks.rs:140`); and `cargo-machete` for unused dependencies. No coverage, no traceability, no deletion experiment, no hotspot ranking in this step (those are Tier 1+ / the gated sibling `code-value-audit-deletion-experiment`).

Mandatory guardrails baked in before any candidate reaches a human (from the skeptic lens, `docs/plans/code-value-audit.explorations/Q-52-skeptic.md`): exclude the CLI / output / pack contract surface (this crate is a PURE BINARY, no `src/lib.rs` / `[lib]`, so there is no downstream Rust API; the contract to exclude is the subcommand / flag / output-format / emitted-pack surface, not arbitrary `pub` items); exclude `#[cfg(...)]`-gated and FFI (`#[no_mangle]` / `extern`) code (a static pass on one cfg is unreliable for these); and carry an explicit "not evidence of absence" caveat on every report ("nothing noticed" is necessary-not-sufficient and only relative to the named signal set, per `docs/plans/code-value-audit.explorations/Q-52-prior-art-survey.md` correction 3). The report is ADVISORY and never auto-deletes; a human decides each candidate and turns accepted deletions into a kickoff task, the same handoff the review entry mode already produces.

Honest scope note (the sharpest skeptic cut): `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` (already required pre-commit) plus rustc `dead_code` already cover most of this cheap case at zero marginal cost, so this step's incremental value over the existing guards is modest; it is scheduled as the cheap, low-false-positive slice that also produces the kept, structured, human-projected report the bare lints do not, and it is the measurement surface for the sibling's evidence gate (counting cases where clippy passed but a deletion experiment would have caught real dead code). Grounded in this repo the rustc cut is sharper than "modest": on a project that gates on `-D warnings` the rustc `dead_code` harvest yields zero candidates, because every latent unused item is `#[allow]`/`#[expect]`-suppressed at source and a command-line lint level cannot override an inner attribute, so the load-bearing value is `cargo-machete` (unused dependencies, the one thing clippy and rustc do not flag) together with the kept, structured report, and the rustc harvest is retained only as the near-free measurement baseline for the sibling's evidence gate (step 87), not a primary candidate source. Judged against the plan principles: Minimal by default (cheap signals only, no engine we do not need), Ground decisions in evidence (per-candidate `file:line` evidence, no heuristic score), Structured data first, project for humans (JSON intermediate -> Markdown), and Prefer the cleaner long-term architecture over the smallest diff (one report, reused by the later deletion-experiment tier). Decided item under `Q-52` (human, 2026-07-24); design record `docs/plans/code-value-audit.explorations/Q-52-multi-signal-design.md`.

### `code-value-audit-deletion-experiment`: the deletion-experiment signal, gated behind an evidence gate (`Q-52`)

Add the DIRECT test of the falsifiable thesis to the code-value report (`code-value-audit-static`): the deletion experiment. Code earns its keep iff removing it causes an OBSERVABLE loss. Two granularities, both run in `checks`'s existing throwaway-worktree machinery (never a second isolation path): function/method granularity via `cargo-mutants` body-nulling (a surviving mutant means no test pins the body, the "pseudo-tested method" of Niedermayr et al.); and item granularity (remove or `#[cfg(any())]`-gate a `struct` / `enum` / `field` / `module`, then `cargo build` + `cargo test`) for kinds `cargo-mutants` does not target. This realizes the reserved `Kind::Mutation` variant (`src/checks.rs:94-95`, `src/checks.rs:671-672`), bounded by the already-parsed `budget` / `threshold` fields (`src/checks.rs:131-142`), scoped ONLY to the shortlist the cheap static signals flagged, never the whole crate.

DEFERRED behind an EVIDENCE GATE. It un-gates only once there is a measured count, from the `code-value-audit-static` report in practice, of cases where `clippy -D warnings` + rustc `dead_code` PASSED but the deletion experiment would have caught real dead code, above a small threshold. Until then the expensive, high-false-positive part stays on the shelf, because the compiler + clippy already cover the cheap case at zero cost and the incremental true-positive rate of the deletion experiment over them is unproven while its false-positive rate is structurally high (public/contract surface, `#[cfg]`-gated code, FFI, and error / defensive paths the test suite does not exercise; see `docs/plans/code-value-audit.explorations/Q-52-skeptic.md`). The debloating soundness numbers quantify the danger of an incomplete oracle (13-22% sound, up to 94% over-removal; `docs/plans/code-value-audit.explorations/Q-52-prior-art-survey.md`), which is why "nothing noticed" stays a candidate, never a proof, and the report never auto-deletes.

Sequencing note: the deletion experiment is structurally a class of mutation operators, so it must not ship as a second mechanism before the mutation module is piloted; building it here IS that pilot, scoped small. Judged against the plan principles: Minimal by default and Ground decisions in evidence hold it behind the gate; Prefer the cleaner long-term architecture over the smallest diff and Reproducible drive the reuse of `checks`'s isolated worktree rather than a parallel path. Decided item under `Q-52` (human, 2026-07-24); design record `docs/plans/code-value-audit.explorations/Q-52-multi-signal-design.md`. Do not build until the gate clears.

### `reviewer-reproducible-evidence`: reviewer findings must carry reproducible evidence proportional to the claim (`Q-66`)

Next (built first, before resuming the paused `code-value-audit-static` step 86). Decided (`Q-66`, Socratic, human, 2026-07-26). Every reviewer finding must carry reproducible evidence PROPORTIONAL to its claim, so a finding is reproduced and adjudicated on its evidence rather than taken on the reviewer's word.

The rule (tiered reproducible evidence). For a BEHAVIORAL or correctness claim (a panic, non-determinism, a wrong output, or "this test is vacuous"), the reviewer provides a RUNNABLE demonstration; the strongest form is a MUTATION, to prove "test T does not really cover code C", break C and show T still passes (the pseudo-tested-method logic). For a DOC, DESIGN, or style claim (stale help text, an em-dash, a naming-collision risk), the reproducible evidence is an EXACT command (grep, diff, or build output) or a `file:line` citation, NOT a contrived test. The evidence is scaled to the claim, so the rule never forces a contrived test where a command or a citation already settles the point. The TRIAGER reproduces whatever the reviewer provided and DISMISSES any testable claim whose demonstration does not reproduce; when that dismissed claim is HIGH or CRITICAL, the dismissal still passes the existing second-triager backstop re-check (`pack/AGENTS.md:59`) before it counts toward a clean round, so the new dismissal ground composes with the backstop rather than bypassing it.

Files the implementer changes:

- `pack/prompts/reviewer.md`: the reviewer authors reproducible evidence proportional to its claim (a runnable or mutation demonstration for a behavioral or correctness claim; an exact command or a `file:line` citation for a doc, design, or style claim), run in the reviewer's own isolated worktree, which every spawned agent already gets under the uniform-isolation rule.
- `pack/prompts/triager.md`: the triager reproduces the provided evidence and dismisses any testable claim whose demonstration does not reproduce.
- `pack/AGENTS.md`: fold the rule into the Reviewers and Triager role bullets and/or the Findings files section, so the guidance and the prompts state one rule.
- Deployed copies (documentation currency): `just scaffold-self` re-renders the root `AGENTS.md`, `.agents/AGENTS.reference.md`, `.agents/prompts/reviewer.md`, and `.agents/prompts/triager.md` from the edited pack, then runs `nix fmt`. The whole-file AGENTS.md drift guard (`agents-md-drift-guard`, step 80) fails if the committed `AGENTS.md` and its `.agents` copy are not a fresh render of the edited `pack/AGENTS.md`, so the regeneration is required, not optional.

Deliberately out of scope: `pack/prompts/checks-reviewer.md` and its `.agents/prompts/checks-reviewer.md` copy. The deterministic checks reviewer already reports every finding with the strongest evidence tier, the check name, the exact command, its exit code, and the offending `file:line`, so it already complies with (indeed exceeds) the tiered rule; the `reviewer.md` + `triager.md` + `pack/AGENTS.md` file set is intentional, not an omission.

Shared machinery with step 87 (the synergy note). The mutation demonstration is the same pseudo-tested-method mechanism the reserved `Kind::Mutation` variant (`src/checks.rs:94-95`) and the deferred `code-value-audit-deletion-experiment` step 87 build on, reusing `checks`'s isolated-worktree machinery; a reviewer runs the demonstration by hand today in its own worktree, and step 87, once its evidence gate opens, is the tool-side automation of the same idea. This step is prompt-and-guidance only: it does NOT build the mutation module or touch `src/checks.rs`, which stays step 87's territory.

Principle grounding (by name). The requirement makes findings falsifiable and checkable, which is Ground decisions in evidence (plan Principle 6) and Reproducible (plan Principle 7, evidence a second party can re-run) applied to the review loop; it is the AGENTS.md workflow guidance "Verify, don't trust" and "Cite sources rather than asserting from memory" made concrete for reviewers, and "Tests must actually exercise the code they claim to" made enforceable through the mutation demonstration. The counterweight is Minimal by default (plan Principle 2): the evidence is proportional, not maximal, so a doc or style claim carries a command or a citation and never a contrived test.

Chosen over a runnable test for EVERY finding (rejected: forces contrived tests for doc and style claims), over a triager-enforced reviewer-SHOULD (rejected: leaves the evidence optional, so a bare assertion can still stand), and over keeping the current process (rejected: a finding can be taken on the reviewer's word). Decision receipt `type:"decision"` `q_id:"Q-66"` in `docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl`.

### `prompt-drift-guard`: extend the whole-file drift guard to the deployed prompt copies

Not started. This is an ENFORCEMENT change in `src/`, not a prose change, and it closes a verified gap rather than settling a design question, so it carries no `[[question]]` and no receipt.

The gap, verified directly rather than taken from the review. `src/agents_md_drift.rs` is the whole-file drift guard, and it covers exactly two files: it embeds `../AGENTS.md` and `../.agents/AGENTS.reference.md` with `include_str!` and compares each against a fresh render of the built-in pack. A sweep of every `include_str!` in `src/` (`recommendation_rule.rs`, `agents_md_drift.rs`, `workflow_spec.rs`, `isolation_policy.rs`, `findings_naming.rs`, `pack.rs`, `plan/source.rs`, `plan/render.rs`, `metrics.rs`) shows that no test embeds or compares any file under `.agents/prompts/`. Those seven prompt copies appear only as destination strings in the scaffolded-asset list (`src/manifest.rs`, the `.agents/prompts/*.md` entries), which asserts WHAT the scaffold emits, never that the COMMITTED copy still matches it. So editing a `pack/prompts/*.md` file and forgetting to regenerate ships a stale deployed prompt and every check stays green. Three review agents reached this independently on step 90's plan review, and step 90 is itself an instance of the exposure: it edits three passages in `pack/prompts/orchestrator.md`, the file that carries most of that change and none of the enforcement.

What the guard must catch (the acceptance-shaped statement for this step):

- Editing any `pack/prompts/<role>.md` without regenerating the deployed `.agents/prompts/<role>.md` MUST fail `cargo test`, with a message naming the file and telling the reader to regenerate.
- A hand edit made directly to a committed `.agents/prompts/<role>.md`, with the pack left alone, MUST also fail. The guard is a two-way correspondence check, not a one-way staleness check.
- An incidental prettier reflow of a committed copy MUST NOT fail, on the same terms the existing guard already accepts for `AGENTS.md` (see the normalisation note below).
- The failure must be demonstrated, not asserted: per the now-live reproducible-evidence rule (`Q-66`, step 88), the implementer breaks the correspondence deliberately (edit one pack prompt, leave the deployed copy stale) and shows the new test fails, then reverts. A guard that cannot be shown to fail is not evidence of anything (plan Principle 6, "Ground decisions in evidence"; the AGENTS.md workflow guidance "Tests must actually exercise the code they claim to").

Reuse, do not reinvent. The existing guard already solved the two hard parts, and both apply unchanged here:

- PRETTIER NORMALISATION. The committed files are `prettier(render output)` because `just scaffold-self` runs the render and then `nix fmt`, whose prettier owns Markdown wrapping at `proseWrap=never`. A raw byte compare would fail on formatter reflow rather than on real drift, so the existing guard passes both sides through `normalize_wrapping` before comparing. The prompt copies live under the same formatter, so the new coverage must use the same normalisation rather than a byte compare.
- THE PRECONDITION FAIL-SAFE (the pattern step 80 established, and the part most likely to be skipped). `normalize_wrapping` is only safe while the guarded text contains no whitespace-significant construct, because it collapses whitespace runs; `assert_no_unprotected_construct` asserts that precondition on BOTH sides and fails loudly the day a nested list, indented code, or a multi-space inline span enters a guarded file, converting a latent masking bug into a visible failure. Any newly guarded file must be run through the same precondition assertion, not just the equality check. Check this against the actual prompt files early: if a prompt already contains such a construct, the precondition will trip immediately, and the answer is to harden `normalize_wrapping` (or exempt that construct deliberately), NOT to drop the assertion.

Implementation choice, decided here rather than left to the implementer. `include_str!` needs a literal path, so covering seven files by the existing pattern means seven more constants and seven more comparisons, which is the enumerated form, and it drifts the moment an eighth prompt is added to the pack. Prefer instead to DERIVE the guarded set from the manifest: render the self-scaffold asset set once, keep every asset whose `dest` starts with `.agents/prompts/`, and compare each against the committed file read from `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`. That makes adding a prompt to the pack automatically guarded, which is the one-source-of-truth form (plan Principle 8, and the AGENTS.md workflow guidance "One source of truth") and is why it is preferred over the smaller enumerated diff (plan Principle 1, "Prefer the cleaner long-term architecture over the smallest diff"). The trade-off to accept knowingly: reading at test time from `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR` is slightly less hermetic than a compile-time `include_str!`, since it reads the working tree rather than a snapshot compiled into the binary. That is acceptable for a repo-local drift guard whose whole purpose is to inspect the working tree, and the existing guard is already repo-local in the same sense. If the implementer finds a concrete reason this does not hold, it is an impasse to raise, not to route around silently.

Scope boundary. Cover `.agents/prompts/` only. The same gap exists for the other copied assets the self-scaffold emits (`.agents/user-prompts/*`, `.agents/LEDGER.template.md`, `.agents/principles.toml`, `.agents/workflow.toml`), and if the derived-from-manifest form above is taken, widening the filter to cover them later is close to free. Do NOT widen it in this step without a human call (the AGENTS.md workflow guidance "No silent scope expansion"); note it in the step's report so the human can decide whether a follow-up is worth it. One asset that must NOT be guarded by this step: `.agents/prompts/checks-reviewer.md` is module-gated (`src/manifest.rs`, emitted only under `--module checks`), and the self-scaffold config the justfile pins uses no modules, so a fresh render under that config does not produce it. A guard that expects it would fail on a correct tree.

Documentation impact. Source and tests only. The step adds no scaffolded content, so no deployed file goes stale and no regeneration is required, which is the reason it can land independently of step 90. Worth a CHANGELOG line if the project's convention covers test-only changes; check what `decision-receipt` and `waiver-model` did before assuming either way.

Interaction with step 90. This step does not block step 90 and step 90 does not block it. Landing this one FIRST would mean step 90's regeneration of `.agents/prompts/orchestrator.md` is enforced rather than trusted, which is the better ordering on the merits; the order as it stands reflects that step 90 is already reviewed and in flight, not a judgement that the guard matters less. If the human wants the enforcement first, reordering costs nothing, since the two touch disjoint files.

### `checks-runner-worktree-name-collision`: make the `checks` runner worktree name unique per call

Deferred. This is a defect fix in `src/`, not a design change: it closes a mechanism verified in the code and observed failing, so it carries no `[[question]]` and no decision receipt. The human's call (2026-07-28) was to TRACK it here rather than schedule it now.

THE MECHANISM, verified in this tree rather than taken from the report.

`run()` names its throwaway worktree from two components, `src/checks.rs:791-792`:

```
let worktree_path =
	std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("{RUNNER_PREFIX}{}-{}", std::process::id(), nanos()));
```

`RUNNER_PREFIX` is the constant `agent-scaffold-checks-run-` (`src/checks.rs:78`), so the full name is `{temp}/agent-scaffold-checks-run-{pid}-{nanos}`. `nanos()` (`src/checks.rs:848-852`) is a bare clock reading with no uniqueness guarantee:

```
std::time::SystemTime::now()
	.duration_since(std::time::UNIX_EPOCH)
	.map_or(0, |elapsed| elapsed.as_nanos())
```

Its own doc comment (`src/checks.rs:845-847`) states the premise that fails: "the process id in the path already provides per-process uniqueness". That is true ACROSS processes and false ACROSS THREADS OF ONE PROCESS. Cargo runs a crate's unit tests as threads of a single test binary, so `std::process::id()` is constant for every test in `checks::tests` and the clock reading is the only thing separating two concurrent `run()` calls.

The clock is not fine-grained enough to carry that alone. Measured on the development machine with a standalone `rustc -O` probe calling the same expression as `nanos()`: consecutive reads on one thread never repeat but advance by a median of 30 ns (minimum 20 ns) over 100000 samples, and two threads sampling concurrently after a shared `Barrier` produce equal values for 8679 of 100000 samples (about 8.7%); at 16 threads it is 568127 of 800000. So the discriminator carries roughly 25 ns of resolution, not 1 ns, and two threads reading it at the same moment agreeing is ordinary rather than exotic. An independent probe during this step's plan review reproduced every one of those numbers and measured the two-thread rate higher still, 10933 to 16386 duplicates per 100000, so read 8.7% as a floor rather than a point estimate.

What a collision then does. Both runs pass the same path to `git worktree add`. Git accepts an EXISTING EMPTY directory as a worktree target and refuses only a non-empty one (verified against git 2.51.2: `git worktree add --detach <pre-created empty dir> HEAD` succeeds; the same command on a directory containing a file fails with `fatal: '<path>' already exists`). Its existence check is not atomic with its creation of the worktree's `.git` pointer file, so two adds issued from DIFFERENT repositories at the same path can both proceed and the later `.git` file overwrites the earlier one. The losing run's isolated tree then points at the winning run's repository, and everything downstream acts on the wrong repo: the tracked-file scan, the check commands, and the `WorktreeGuard` cleanup at `src/checks.rs:329-342`, which unregisters and `remove_dir_all`s the shared directory while the other run is still inside it. The recorded failure text below (both tests citing one path, each error naming the OTHER test's fixture repository) is what that looks like from the outside.

The same collision has a SECOND presentation, and a future sighting is more likely to take that shape, so do not expect only the take-over. When the two adds do not interleave the wrong way, one or both simply fail, because `git worktree add` refuses a non-empty directory: in `run()` that becomes `RunError::WorktreeSetup` (`src/checks.rs:795-800`), and at the fixtures it is a `git_ok` assertion failure. A paired race driven at one shared path during this step's plan review split 200 collisions into 25 where both adds succeeded (the cross-registered take-over above, with the path registered in both repositories in every one of the 25), 160 where exactly one succeeded, and 15 where neither did. So the loud failure is the common shape and the silent cross-linking is the minority; both are this one mechanism.

EVIDENCE IT IS REAL, not theoretical.

Observed once in six consecutive runs during the step-92 (`prompt-drift-guard`) round-2 triage, quoted here verbatim because its findings file is transient and will be removed under the commit-before-delete rule (it was `docs/plans/agent-scaffold.reviews/prompt-drift-guard-r2-triage.md` at commit `9f0966c`, recoverable from history):

> My first `cargo test` in this worktree failed `checks::tests::a_format_check_never_mutates_the_live_tree` and `checks::tests::an_empty_paths_array_runs_unscoped`; five later runs passed. Both failures cited the SAME runner worktree path, `agent-scaffold-checks-run-416707-1785235883764925866`, and each error named the OTHER test's fixture repo.

The shared path is the whole proof: one pid (`416707`), one nanosecond value (`1785235883764925866`), two tests.

Corroboration, and the reason this is not the first sighting. The ledger's RESUME STATE records, from the `code-value-audit-static` inc1 review: "A rare pre-existing MAIN-binary test-parallelism flake was seen once in inc1 review (candidate backlog item on test isolation)." (quoted by text, not line, since the ledger is edited in place and line citations into it rot). That note had a symptom and no mechanism; this finding supplies the mechanism. Which tests failed on that earlier occasion is not recorded, so treat the identification as probable rather than certain; what is certain is that the recorded history now has two sightings, not one, which is the argument against filing this as noise.

SEVERITY, BOUNDED HONESTLY IN BOTH DIRECTIONS.

Production is NOT affected. Each `agent-scaffold checks` invocation is its own process, so two concurrent runs have different pids and their names cannot collide while both are alive. The concurrency case that DOES arise in production, two overlapping runs on the same repository, is already handled by the pid-liveness gate on the startup prune (`src/checks.rs:407-461`), which is not implicated here; nor is its benign pid-reuse edge (`src/checks.rs:425-428`). Read that as a statement about the SHIPPED path only: the live pid separates two processes at `src/checks.rs:791-792`, but it separates nothing at the two constant-pid test fixtures (see the scope section), which never run outside `cargo test`.

The test suite IS affected. Every unit test shares one pid, so the only discriminator is the ~25 ns clock. The damage is not a shipped defect, it is that `cargo test` is not deterministically green, which corrodes the evidence base the whole review process rests on: every convergence decision in this repo reads a green suite as a settled fact, and a suite that fails about one run in six makes a green summary line a claim about luck. Do not escalate this to a user-facing bug, and do not dismiss it as cosmetic; it sits exactly between.

SCOPE: WHERE THE DEFECT LIVES.

The collision surface is any path whose only discriminator is a clock reading. In this tree that is:

- `src/checks.rs:791-792`, the production runner path, exercised concurrently by the `checks::tests` cases that call `run()` (22 call sites in that module).
- `src/checks.rs:1462`, `src/checks.rs:1491`, and `src/checks.rs:1492`, test fixtures that build `{RUNNER_PREFIX}{pid}-{nanos}` names by hand in the SAME namespace. Exactly ONE of them carries the live pid: `:1491` uses `std::process::id()`, while `:1462` and `:1492` use `dead_pid()`, the compile-time constant `u32::MAX` (`src/checks.rs:1438-1442`). So `:1491` can collide with a concurrent real `run()` and with the other fixtures, and the two constant-pid sites can collide with each other in-process. The constant-pid pair is also the only place in this tree that carries no CROSS-PROCESS discriminator at all: their first segment is the same constant in every process, so two concurrent `cargo test` processes (this project's normal state, with several worktrees in play) share the whole template and have only the clock between them. A fix that touches only `run()` leaves all of that in place.

Those two sites MUST keep a dead pid; it is a design constraint, not an oversight to correct. `dead_pid()` asserts `!pid_is_alive(pid)` because the tests exist to plant an orphan owned by a dead owner so the prune reclaims it, and `owning_pid` (`src/checks.rs:400-405`) reads the FIRST `-`-separated segment. Any discriminator that separates two PROCESSES there therefore has to be appended AFTER the constant pid: a `create_dir` reservation, entropy, or even the live pid as a later component (`{RUNNER_PREFIX}{dead_pid}-{live_pid}-{seq}` still parses as a dead owner). That is named to show the constraint is cheap to satisfy, not to pre-decide the fix.

Checked and NOT affected, so the step does not widen into them: the other scratch helpers discriminate by a per-test literal name rather than by the clock and so are unique by construction (`src/checks.rs:862-871`, `src/main.rs:2280-2285`, `src/manifest.rs:552-558`, `src/plan/render.rs:638`, `tests/audit_command.rs:20`, `tests/scaffold_precommit_hook.rs:14`, `tests/checks_staged_hook_env.rs:50`). Integration-test sites do use `{pid}-{nanos}`, but each carries a distinct literal prefix, so they cannot collide today; they are a latent copy-paste hazard to note, not to fix here.

WHAT "DONE" LOOKS LIKE.

- The runner worktree path is unique per call BY CONSTRUCTION, and the argument for why is written in the code comment, since the current comment is precisely where the wrong argument was written down.
- The name is generated in ONE place and used by both `run()` and the three fixtures, so a fixture cannot drift from the production naming (plan Principle 1, prefer the cleaner long-term architecture over the smallest diff: a shared generator, not a patch to the single line that happened to be caught failing).
- `owning_pid` (`src/checks.rs:400-405`) still parses the owning pid. It takes the first `-`-separated segment after the prefix, so the pid must stay the FIRST component and any new component is appended after it; the prune's liveness gate reads nothing else.
- Every comment the documentation-impact section below names is corrected in the same change.
- The uniqueness property is pinned by a test that FAILS without the fix (see the demonstration section, which is the load-bearing part of this step).

CANDIDATE FIXES AND THEIR TRADE-OFFS. Not pre-decided here; the implementer picks one and argues it, or raises the choice if it is a genuine fork.

- (a) A process-wide atomic counter, `{pid}-{nanos}-{seq}` from a `static AtomicU64`. Zero dependencies, unique by construction within a process, smallest diff, keeps the pid first. It closes every in-process channel, including both fixture namespaces, and those are the channels that produced the observed failure. Weakness: it guarantees nothing across processes, and two processes start their counter at the same value. Where the pid is live that is no worse than today, since two live processes hold different pids, and it leaves only the pid-reuse edge the existing prune already treats as benign (`src/checks.rs:425-428`). That argument does NOT hold at the two constant-pid fixtures (`src/checks.rs:1462` and `:1492`), where the first segment is `u32::MAX` in every process and so discriminates nothing: there (a) alone leaves two concurrent `cargo test` processes with identical name templates and the clock as their only separation. That channel is genuinely rare, since a hit needs two independently launched processes to reach the same `format!` within about 25 ns, so of order 1e-6 per pair; an attempt to reproduce it cross-process during this step's plan review found 0 in 40 pairs, which is the expected result whether or not the channel exists and so is not evidence either way. It is not a reason to reject (a); it is the reason to choose between (a) alone and the (a) + (d) composition below deliberately, and to say in the commit which channels the chosen fix closes and which it leaves.
- (b) A random suffix. There is no public RNG in std, so this means adding `rand` for a filename suffix. That is out of proportion for this repo's dependency discipline, which the code itself states at `src/checks.rs:388-392` (no libc pulled in just for a `kill(pid, 0)`); the std workaround (`RandomState` / `DefaultHasher`) is obscure for what it buys. Cheapest to write, worst cost/benefit.
- (c) `std::thread::current().id()`. Zero dependencies and it targets the observed case directly. But `ThreadId` exposes no stable textual form (`as_u64` is unstable, leaving `Debug`'s `ThreadId(3)`, which is neither documented as stable nor filename-safe without sanitising), and it discriminates THREADS, not CALLS, so two calls on one thread fall back on the clock again. Strictly weaker than (a) at the same cost.
- (d) Let the filesystem enforce it: reserve the path with `std::fs::create_dir` (one `mkdir`, which fails with `AlreadyExists` atomically rather than racing) and retry with a fresh name on collision, then hand the reserved empty directory to `git worktree add`. Strongest guarantee, since uniqueness stops depending on any entropy argument and covers the cross-process and pid-reuse cases too, and zero new dependencies. Verified compatible with git: `git worktree add --detach` into a pre-created EMPTY directory succeeds (git 2.51.2), which is the objection that would otherwise sink this option. Costs a retry loop and one extra syscall. A `tempfile`-crate version of the same idea adds a dependency and buys nothing over the std form here.

(a) and (d) compose: a counter for the name plus `create_dir` as the reservation gives both a cheap unique name and a loud failure the day the uniqueness argument is wrong (plan Principle 5, make illegal states unrepresentable, applied to a path namespace).

THE DEMONSTRATION PROBLEM. This is the hardest part of the step and the part most likely to be skipped.

The reproducible-evidence rule (`Q-66`, step 88) is live, and this claim is behavioural, so the implementer owes a runnable demonstration, ideally the mutation form: break the code and show the test still passes. Plan Principle 6 (ground decisions in evidence) is the standard the demonstration is judged against, and it is not met by a green suite here, for the reason below.

"I ran `cargo test` and it was green" is exactly the non-evidence that rule exists to reject. Work the arithmetic on the one rate that was measured, one failure in six runs. Under UNCHANGED code the chance of six consecutive green runs is (5/6)^6 = 0.33, so a six-run green streak is roughly a coin flip and proves nothing. To reach 95% confidence that a 1-in-6 failure mode is gone takes 17 consecutive clean runs ((5/6)^n <= 0.05 first holds at n = 17). And that 1-in-6 is a single sample from one machine, so the true rate is unknown and varies with core count and clock granularity; the run-count argument is therefore even weaker than its own arithmetic. If a run-count claim is made at all, it must state the number of runs and the confidence bound it actually supports.

The way out is to stop sampling the probabilistic event and test the deterministic property underneath it:

- Name the unit under test by the PROPERTY, not by the function. What must be demonstrated is that no two concurrent RESERVATIONS resolve to the same worktree path, whatever supplies the uniqueness. So test the call that yields the final path, the one `run()` and the fixtures actually use: N threads released together on a `std::sync::Barrier`, each taking M paths, then assert N * M distinct paths and no error. Stated that way the test is green against any of (a), (b), (c), (d) implemented correctly, and red against today's code. Stated as "the name GENERATOR returns N * M distinct strings" it is not: under (d) the uniqueness lives in the `create_dir` reservation and the raw name still duplicates at the clock's rate, measured at 2793 to 3354 duplicates in 8000 at N = 8, M = 1000, so a string-level assertion is red against a CORRECT (d) and would push an implementer into adding entropy that fix does not need.
- Show the property covers the real construction sites, or it proves nothing about them. A test that pins a new generator while the inline `format!` at `src/checks.rs:791-792`, or a fixture's own `format!`, survives beside it is green with the defect fully present, which is exactly the shape the AGENTS.md principle "Tests must actually exercise the code they claim to" names, and it is the state the three fixtures are in today. A command settles this and no extra test is owed (`Q-66` proportionality): show that exactly one `format!` in `src/checks.rs` builds a `RUNNER_PREFIX` name, reconciled against the sites the scope section enumerates.
- Show it RED before green: run the property test against the unfixed path-yielding call, or mutate the fix's disambiguator to a constant, and show it fails; then restore. That mutation is what separates a test that pins the property from a test that merely passes, and it is the form `Q-66` names as strongest.
- Optional higher-fidelity extra, if the linkage command above is judged too indirect: drive two `run()` calls from two threads with the path generation forced to a common value, and show the pre-fix build produces the cross-repository `.git` corruption (or the `WorktreeSetup` failure, which is the more common shape) while the post-fix build does not. It forces generation through `run()` itself, so it settles the linkage rather than arguing it; the cost is real machinery, and the requirements above are the proportional minimum.
- Report the measured numbers, not the word "fixed".

RELATION TO STEP 85 (`drift-guard-test-hook-hygiene`). Same family, different defect, and they must not be merged into one step.

Step 85 is a process-global panic-hook swap in `src/agents_md_drift.rs`: diagnostic-only, it cannot change any test's pass or fail, and its cost is a lost backtrace. This step is a shared-path collision in `src/checks.rs` that HAS changed test outcomes, twice in the recorded history. They touch disjoint files and neither blocks the other, so doing both in one sitting is cheap and sensible. Doing them as ONE step is not: their evidence burdens differ, since 85's fix is unobservable from test outcomes while this one owes the red/green uniqueness demonstration above, and bundling them lets 85's easy "no behaviour change" story stand in for the harder one. If both are scheduled, this one goes first, because it is the one that makes the suite lie.

DOCUMENTATION IMPACT: in-code only.

The change must correct four comments in `src/checks.rs`: `:72-77` (`RUNNER_PREFIX`) and `:400-402` (`owning_pid`), which spell the name format; `:845-847` (`nanos`), which states the false per-process-uniqueness premise; and `:789-790`, the comment on the naming site itself, which asserts the same false uniqueness ("A unique temp path OUTSIDE the repository ... The `RUNNER_PREFIX` (with the embedded pid) is what the startup prune recognises"). The same implementer corrects all of them, so no separate documentation step is owed. Nothing scaffolded changes: the temp path is an internal implementation detail, not part of the CLI, the output, or the pack contract, so `AGENTS.md`, `pack/`, and the deployed `.agents/` copies are untouched and no regeneration is required. Outside the plan's own documents the name format is written down only in `src/`: `README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, and `pack/` carry no occurrence of `agent-scaffold-checks-run`, and every `docs/` occurrence is inside this plan's own material recording this defect, so nothing outside `src/` goes stale when the name format changes. A CHANGELOG `Fixed` entry is likely right, but the `Unreleased` section currently carries only `Added` and `Changed`, so check what a comparable internal-only fix did before assuming either way.

### `workflow-enforcement-tier`: anchor the metrics log and the ledger to the plan source, refuse an unsafe pairing, fail when `--workflow` cannot run, and document the two enforcement tiers (`Q-55`)

Four defects, one family. They all came from the same root cause (the tool decided which project's data to read from the process working directory rather than from the plan it was handed) or from the same undocumented boundary (a project that did not opt into `--instrument` was promised enforcement it could not get). Every reproduction below was produced by running the tool, first by the planner on 2026-07-31, then re-run independently by three explorers in a build-and-measure design pass, then in two cases re-run first-hand by the orchestrator on main. Nothing here is quoted from the `Q-44` audit.

- DEFECT A, THE FALSE GREEN. `Q-55` proper (the `SE-3` two-tier enforcement gap): a project with no metrics log got exit 0 from a check that never ran.
- DEFECT B, CROSS-PROJECT CONTAMINATION. Not in `Q-55`'s text and worse: the metrics-log path resolved against the current working directory, so the check could join one project's plan to another project's log and declare the invariants hold.
- DEFECT C, THE SIBLING COMMANDS. `status`, `next`, and the derived ledger path carried the identical resolution defect. `next` did not degrade to an empty projection, it emitted a fabricated instruction to close an unreviewed step, and `status --resume` printed one project's internal resume state into another project's agent brief.
- DEFECT D, THE `SE-3` DOCUMENTATION HALF. The scaffolded `AGENTS.md` promised the `validate --workflow` backstop without qualification, so a user who scaffolded without `--instrument` read a promise of deterministic enforcement they do not have and, after this step, cannot get without being told why the tool now refuses.

PROVENANCE. `Q-55`, decided by the human on 2026-07-31, with decision receipts in `docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl`, all carrying `task:"workflow-enforcement-tier"`.

`Q-55-mechanism` and `Q-55-noconvention` closed a DESIGN PASS whose three records are committed at `docs/plans/workflow-enforcement-tier.explorations/` (1514 lines: `metrics-path-anchor-to-source.md` 521, `metrics-path-plan-declared.md` 483, `metrics-path-independent-map.md` 510). Three worktree-isolated explorers each BUILT a candidate in a scratch copy and MEASURED it rather than arguing it on paper, and the narrative of the pass is in `docs/plans/agent-scaffold.ledger.md` in the paragraphs beginning "THE DESIGN PASS IS DONE (2026-07-31) AND ALL THREE RECORDS ARE ON MAIN" through "TWO HUMAN DECISIONS CLOSED THE DESIGN PASS (2026-07-31)". The pass's own headline, worth carrying because it is what makes its conclusions load-bearing rather than advisory: "BOTH BUILDERS ARGUED AGAINST THE CANDIDATE THEY WERE TOLD TO BUILD".

The first pass scoped two defects and two increments, correctly for what was then known. Two human scope additions (defects C and D), the design pass, and further human decisions all landed after it. Its increment set, its risk classifications, and three of its factual claims are superseded here; the corrections are marked in place so a reader who saw the earlier version can find them.

## The fixture, shared by every reproduction

A throwaway non-instrumented project, which is what every new adopter is by definition:

```sh
agent-scaffold scaffold --output-dir "$SCRATCH" --write --force --principles default
```

That drops 30 files ("Wrote to $SCRATCH (30 changed, 0 left untouched)") and NO `docs/metrics/` directory: `ls "$SCRATCH/docs"` prints only `plans`. The instrumentation asset is gated behind `--instrument`, which is off by default (`src/main.rs:ScaffoldArgs::instrument`), so the round log the workflow check reads does not exist. All three explorers rebuilt this fixture from scratch and all three confirmed the missing `docs/metrics/` independently.

## Defect A, the false green (`Q-55` proper)

Run from INSIDE the fixture:

```sh
cd "$SCRATCH"
agent-scaffold validate --source docs/plans/TEMPLATE.plan.toml --workflow
```

Observed, with the streams separated:

```
stdout: docs/plans/TEMPLATE.plan.toml: 1 steps, 0 questions, valid
stderr: no metrics log at docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl; nothing to validate
stderr: --workflow has a plan source but the metrics log is missing; skipping the workflow check
exit:   0
```

CORRECTION TO `Q-55`'S OWN WORDING, which the implementer should not carry forward. `Q-55` says `validate --workflow` "silently passes". That WAS an OVERSTATEMENT: the skip WAS announced, twice, both in `src/main.rs:run_validate` (the `no metrics log at <path>; nothing to validate` note, and the `--workflow has a plan source but the metrics log is missing; skipping the workflow check` note that inc3 replaced with a reported problem). The correction is sharper than it first looks, because both announcements WENT to STDERR (both WERE `eprintln!`), while the only thing on stdout WAS the ok summary. The operative defect WAS therefore the EXIT CODE and nothing else: a CI gate reads the exit status, not the stderr log, so `validate --workflow` RETURNED success for a project with zero machine enforcement of any workflow invariant. Write it up as a false green, never as a silent one. Explorer B captured the streams separately at the pre-change build and confirmed stderr empty on the defect-B invocation and non-empty here, which is what makes the distinction measured rather than asserted.

THE MECHANISM. The `--workflow` block is a four-arm `match` in `src/main.rs:run_validate` over `(toml_primary, &plan_contents, &metrics_contents)`. The arm that FIRED here WAS that match's `_` catch-all, which PRINTED the skip note and PUSHED NO problem, so `problems` STAYED empty and `run_validate` TOOK its `if problems.is_empty()` success branch.

THE DECIDED REMEDY (human, 2026-07-31, receipt `q_id:"Q-55"`): FAIL WHEN `--workflow` CANNOT RUN. When `--workflow` is explicitly requested and no metrics log exists at the resolved path, the run exits non-zero and reports why. Plain `validate` (and `validate --source` / `--plan` without `--workflow`) is UNAFFECTED: an absent log there stays a stderr note and exit 0, because nobody asked for the check. The reasoning the human accepted: the user explicitly asked for the workflow check, so skipping it and reporting success is the defect. The policy applies to the resolved metrics path however it was resolved, whether from the anchored default or from an explicit `--metrics` value; "the user named a path that does not exist" is not a weaker case than "the default path does not exist".

WHAT WAS REJECTED, AND WHY. Make round-logging CORE rather than opt-in: rejected as forcing instrumentation on users who did not ask for it, and a substantially bigger change than the defect warrants (Minimal by default; the `--instrument` opt-in is the two-tier design working as intended, not the bug). Warn but keep exit 0: rejected because a warning with exit 0 is still green in CI, which is the actual failure mode being fixed; it would leave the defect in place and add a message beside it.

THE PRECEDENT THIS FOLLOWS, ALREADY IN THE TREE, so this is closing the second half of a hole whose first half is already closed. The sibling `(None, None, _)` arm of `src/main.rs:run_validate`'s `--workflow` match handles "`--workflow` requested but no plan source resolved" and pushes a hard problem, with the comment stating the identical reasoning: "`--workflow` was explicitly requested, so skipping would green-pass while checking nothing; make it a hard problem instead." That arm was itself a false-green fix (Inc 6, finding M-1) and is pinned by `tests/validate_workflow_toml_source_needs_no_plan.rs:127-171`. Defect A is the same defect on the other input, and the fix is the same shape.

A CASE THAT IS NOT PART OF THIS, named so the work does not creep into it. A metrics log that is PRESENT but EMPTY is not a false green and needs no change: the check runs, and W3 fails on any `complete` step with no round records (demonstrated in the acceptance check below). The missing-file case is different in kind because the check does not run at all.

## Defect B, cross-project contamination

Not in `Q-55`'s text, found only by running the tool, and a straight bug independent of whichever tier policy was chosen. Run from the agent-scaffold repository root against the fixture's plan:

```sh
cd /path/to/agent-scaffold
agent-scaffold validate --source "$SCRATCH/docs/plans/TEMPLATE.plan.toml" --workflow
```

Observed (the record count grows as the log accumulates; the planner's first reproduction read 233, the second 235, and explorers A, B and C all reproduced 235 independently at their own base commits):

```
stdout: docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl: 235 records, valid
stdout: $SCRATCH/docs/plans/TEMPLATE.plan.toml: 1 steps, 0 questions, valid
stdout: $SCRATCH/docs/plans/TEMPLATE.plan.toml vs docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl: workflow invariants hold
exit:   0
```

Those 235 records are AGENT-SCAFFOLD'S OWN log, joined against a foreign one-step plan, and the join was declared to hold. The green is not merely empty, it is affirmatively wrong: it asserts an invariant over a pairing of two unrelated projects.

THE SHARPER DEMONSTRATION, which turns "wrong pairing" into a measurable FALSE PASS and is the red case the increment's test must pin. Give the fixture's single step a slug that has round records in agent-scaffold's log, and mark it complete:

```sh
cd "$SCRATCH"
# in docs/plans/TEMPLATE.plan.toml, on the single [[step]]:
#   slug   = "example-step"    -> "triager-runs-only-on-findings"
#   status = "not-started"     -> "complete"
cp docs/plans/TEMPLATE.steps/example-step.md docs/plans/TEMPLATE.steps/triager-runs-only-on-findings.md
```

The fixture now claims a completed, reviewed step and has no review evidence of its own whatsoever. From the agent-scaffold root, `agent-scaffold validate --source "$SCRATCH/docs/plans/TEMPLATE.plan.toml" --workflow` still printed `workflow invariants hold` and exited 0. Agent-scaffold's own rounds for its step 78 satisfied a foreign project's convergence claim. Explorer C reproduced the same false pass with a different borrowed slug (`agents-md-drift-guard`), which is worth noting because it establishes the defect is a property of the join and not of one lucky slug.

THE CONTROL, which proves the check itself is sound and the defect is purely in which file it reads. From inside the fixture, with an empty log so the check can run against the RIGHT project:

```sh
cd "$SCRATCH" && mkdir -p docs/metrics && : > docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl
agent-scaffold validate --source docs/plans/TEMPLATE.plan.toml --workflow
```

```
stderr: docs/plans/TEMPLATE.plan.toml vs docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl: Roadmap step `triager-runs-only-on-findings` is `complete` but has no round records and no covering waiver; log its review rounds, or record a `type:"waiver"` for it if it predates logging or its review was skipped
exit:   1
```

All three explorers re-ran this control and all three got the same red. The check is sound; it was handed the wrong file.

THE MECHANISM IN THE CODE. `--metrics` WAS declared with a RELATIVE default, `#[arg(long, default_value = "docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl")]` at `src/main.rs:ValidateArgs::metrics`, and every use of it (`metrics_path.exists()` and `fs::read_to_string`, both in `src/main.rs:run_validate`) RESOLVED that relative path against the PROCESS working directory. The `--source` path WAS taken as given. Nothing anywhere RECONCILED the two, so the pairing of plan and log WAS an accident of where the user happened to stand. `check_workflow_toml` (`src/workflow.rs:180-195`) then joins whatever it is handed, and W3 matches a round to a step by SLUG alone (`round_step_slug(round) == step.slug`, `src/workflow.rs:448-449`), with no project identity anywhere in the record or the join, which is why a borrowed slug is enough.

THE REQUIRED END PROPERTY, which is what "done" means for this half regardless of the mechanism: `validate --workflow` must never pair a plan source with a metrics log belonging to a different project and report success. Where the tool cannot establish that the two belong together, it must say so and exit non-zero rather than proceed. A run made from the plan's own project root with a bare relative `--source`, which is the normal invocation, must be unchanged (Safe on existing projects), except for the symlink divergence recorded below as accepted cost (ii).

THE DESIGN PASS'S SHARPEST RESULT ON THIS POINT, and the reason the mechanism is anchor PLUS refusal rather than anchor alone: explorer A finished building the anchor and then attacked its own build, producing TWO FURTHER false passes against it, one with an explicit RELATIVE `--metrics` and one through a SYMLINKED plan source, both printing `workflow invariants hold` at exit 0 for a foreign project with no review evidence. Explorer C reached the first of those independently as its attack 4, by a different route and on a different model, which the ledger records as "THAT IS THE PASS'S STRONGEST CONVERGENCE". A's framing is the load-bearing part: shipping the anchor alone closes the KNOWN REPRODUCTION and leaves the DEFECT CLASS open, which is the worst available outcome, because the next reader will believe it fixed.

## Defect C, the sibling commands

CORRECTION TO THE FIRST PLANNER PASS, and the most consequential of the three. That pass named `status` (`src/main.rs:StatusArgs::metrics`), `next` (`src/main.rs:NextArgs::metrics`) and `default_ledger_path` (`src/main.rs`) as carrying the identical CWD-relative defect, raised their inclusion for the human, and argued they were separable because "Both are best-effort projections rather than validators, so a wrong path there yields an empty projection rather than a false assertion, which is why they are separable." THAT REASONING IS FALSE. It was falsified independently by two explorers using different mechanisms, and then re-verified first-hand by the orchestrator on main rather than relayed.

`next` DID NOT DEGRADE TO EMPTY. It reads the round log to project the ACTIVE LOOP: the round number, the convergence state, the clean-round streak, the role to spawn next, and the instruction. Handed a foreign log it emitted a confident and completely fabricated instruction. Reproduced by the orchestrator at commit `3170e3f` against a scaffolded non-instrumented fixture whose single step slug was set to `triager-runs-only-on-findings` and whose status was `in-progress`, run from the agent-scaffold root:

```
metrics: 235 records
state: converged
streak: 1/1
rounds: 2/5
next: mark the step complete, re-render, and commit
exit: 0
```

for a project with ZERO rounds of its own. Explorer A produced the same shape on its own fixture (`state: converged`, `rounds: 2/5`, `next: mark the step complete, re-render, and commit`) and the post-fix contrast on the same build (`metrics: 0 records`, `state: awaiting-first-review`, `streak: 0/?`, `rounds: 0/5`, `next: spawn a reviewer for the first review round`).

`status --resume` IS A THIRD CASE AND IT IS NOT A WRONG NUMBER AT ALL. Explorer B renamed a fixture's plan file to `agent-scaffold.plan.toml` (the ledger path derives `<task>` from the plan source FILENAME, so any foreign project whose plan file collides gets this) and ran `status --resume` from this repository's root. It printed THIS repository's entire `## RESUME STATE` block verbatim, branch names, worktree paths and in-flight review state included, as the resume anchor for an unrelated project. `next` echoed the same block into the instruction it hands an agent.

THE ASYMMETRY, which is why the projections are arguably the MORE urgent half and not the milder one. `validate --workflow`'s false green misled a HUMAN who may or may not be reading. `next`'s false instruction was consumed by an AGENT that acts on it, and the instruction it fabricated was "mark the step complete", which is precisely the false completion the whole convergence apparatus exists to prevent. `status --resume` was not a wrong boolean at all but CONTENT INJECTION into an instruction that the receiving agent has been told is authoritative and to read first. The human added the siblings to scope before this evidence existed; the evidence bears on their ORDER, not merely on their inclusion.

CORRECTION TO THE FIRST PASS'S CLAIM ABOUT `default_ledger_path`. That pass said it "already assumes the `<root>/docs/plans/<task>.plan.toml` layout". IT DID NOT. It ASSUMED THE CURRENT DIRECTORY WAS THE ROOT (`PathBuf::from(format!("docs/plans/{task}.ledger.md"))`, `src/main.rs:default_ledger_path`) and BROKE as soon as it was not. Explorer A established this by running, not reading: from inside `docs/plans` with a bare `--source`, the pre-fix build looked for `<root>/docs/plans/docs/plans/p.ledger.md` and reported "no ledger", for a ledger that exists. A adds the simplification that follows: the ledger NEEDS NO ROOT DERIVATION AT ALL, because it lives BESIDE the plan, so the source's own directory is the whole rule. That is simpler than the metrics rule and has fewer cases that can go wrong: no upward walk, no fallback branch, no convention to miss.

## Defect D, the `SE-3` documentation half

Verified by running, not by reading the pack. The NON-instrumented scaffold's `AGENTS.md` CONTAINED, verbatim:

```
the deterministic `validate --workflow` check, once built, is the backstop that the required reviewed rounds happened before a step is marked complete.
```

That sentence WAS rendered from `pack/AGENTS.md:93`, in the "Worktree lifecycle and merge-back" paragraph, and it WAS UNCONDITIONAL. The only two places `pack/AGENTS.md` mentions `docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl` outside the instrumentation section are `pack/AGENTS.md:61` and `:63`, both inside "When instrumentation is on" clauses, and the whole round-log schema lives in `pack/instrument.md`, which is rendered into the `{{instrument}}` slot at `pack/AGENTS.md:116` ONLY under `--instrument` (its own closing line says so: "This section is present only because instrumentation was enabled; a scaffold without `--instrument` omits it entirely"). So a user who SCAFFOLDED without `--instrument` READ a promise of a deterministic backstop, GOT no `docs/metrics/` directory, and GOT exit 0 from the check that was supposed to provide it.

THIS STEP WOULD HAVE MADE THE GAP WORSE BEFORE IT FIXED IT, which is why the documentation is not optional garnish. After the tier policy landed, that same non-instrumented user would not have got a quiet false green any more: they would have got a hard failure from a check the guidance told them was their backstop, with nothing in the guidance explaining that the backstop is tier-two. An unqualified promise plus a new hard error is a worse reading experience than an unqualified promise plus a quiet skip. The documentation half must therefore land in the SAME increment as the tier policy, not after it.

## The mechanism, decided rather than chosen here

`Q-55-mechanism` (human, 2026-07-31, receipt `q_id:"Q-55-mechanism"`): ANCHOR PLUS REFUSAL, IDENTITY QUEUED. Ship candidate (a), the metrics path anchored to the plan source, PLUS a refusal for unsafe pairings, covering `validate`, `next`, `status` and the ledger path, and QUEUE project identity in the round record to the validation-constraints step. The human declined both the wider option (identity fields in the same step) and the narrower one (anchor only). The recorded reasoning: the pass measured that anchoring alone leaves the DEFECT CLASS open, so the refusal is not gold-plating, while pulling identity in would edit the record schema that W3, W4 and W5 all read, which the calibration close already argued should be ONE deliberate edit rather than a rider on a path fix.

The implementer does NOT re-open any of the following. Each is recorded with the measurement that settled it.

DISTINGUISHING A DEFAULTED `--metrics` FROM AN EXPLICIT ONE: use `Option<PathBuf>` with a bare `#[arg(long)]`, and apply the default after resolution. Do NOT use clap's `ArgMatches::value_source`. The reason is NOT the 17 lines saved. Explorer A built both routes to a working state and then FORCED the `value_source` failure mode by renaming the argument id, simulating a later field rename. Both the subcommand and the argument are addressed by STRING, so in a DEBUG build clap panics (`` `"metrics_typo"` is not an id of an argument or a group ``, exit 101) while in a RELEASE build the same code silently answers "not supplied", so the user's explicit `--metrics docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl` is IGNORED and a different file is read with no message. That is a debug/release behaviour divergence, guarded only by clap's `debug_assertions`, in the code path whose entire purpose is deciding which file to read: the same self-concealing class as the defect under repair, which is what makes it disqualifying rather than merely uglier. Two lesser measured costs: `value_source` is `+96/-13` against `Option<PathBuf>`'s `+79/-15` for identical behaviour, and clap prints the `default_value` it was given with no way to keep the value and suppress the display, so `--help` would carry a now-false `[default: docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl]`. This independently vindicates Make illegal states unrepresentable, which A was told to TEST rather than repeat.

THE DERIVATION: a purely LEXICAL, NEAREST-WINS upward search. Start at the source's parent directory and walk up; the first ancestor whose own file name is `plans` and whose parent's file name is `docs` identifies `<root>/docs/plans`, and the root is that ancestor's grandparent. No filesystem access and no canonicalisation. The metrics default is then `<root>/docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl`. With neither a `--source` nor a `--plan` there is nothing to anchor to, so the historical CWD-relative path stands unchanged.

THE CONVENTIONLESS CASE, decided by `Q-55-noconvention` (receipt `q_id:"Q-55-noconvention"`): when no `docs/plans`-shaped ancestor exists, FALL BACK TO THE SOURCE'S OWN DIRECTORY, with the containment refusal layered on top. Chosen over a hard error. A had MEASURED the fallback resolving the `--source myplan.plan.toml`-at-a-repository-root case correctly, both from that root and from elsewhere, and Safe on existing projects favours resolving a legitimate layout over rejecting it. This is the case the first planner pass called "no convention to lean on"; there is one, and it is the same answer the CWD-relative default would have given from the right directory.

WHAT THE DERIVATION WAS MEASURED AGAINST. A built a case matrix in which every candidate log location carries a DIFFERENT record count, so the printed count identifies which file was actually read, then ran it. The `docs/plans` convention resolves correctly in every spelling constructed: absolute, relative, `./`-prefixed, and with a `..` that stays below the project's own `docs/plans` (that last works because `Path::file_name` returns `None` for a `..` component, so the walk skips past it and reaches that project's `docs/plans` above it). A plan at a root with no `docs/plans` resolves through the fallback. A subdirectory under `docs/plans` resolves to the project root. The rule never consults `.git`, so a nested repository and a directory outside any repository behave identically and correctly; "project root" here is a FILENAME CONVENTION, not a VCS fact, which is a feature (no VCS dependency, works in a tarball) and should be written up as one. ONE CASE IS A JUDGEMENT CALL AND IS RECORDED AS SUCH: a second `docs/plans` in the parent chain resolves NEAREST-WINS to the inner project. A chose it on the reasoning that the innermost project owns the plan, and reported it as "the only place I chose between two defensible answers without external evidence". It is not evidenced; an implementer or reviewer may revisit it on evidence, and must not treat it as settled by measurement. NOT IN THAT MATRIX, AND MEASURED AT WORK REVIEW: a `..` that climbs OUT through a `docs/plans` matches THAT directory, so `<root>/docs/plans/../../other/p.plan.toml` and `<root>/other/p.plan.toml` are the same file read against two different logs. It follows from the lexical rule rather than being a defect in it, it is not a regression (before anchoring, both spellings read the current directory's log), and it is the canonical guard in inc2, whose root comes from the REAL (canonicalised) location of the plan the check reads, which in that spelling is the source itself, that rejects it.

THE REFUSAL (candidate (b), layered on top). Before the four-arm match in `run_validate`'s `--workflow` block, derive the root from the REAL (canonicalised) location of THE PLAN THE CHECK READS, which is available BEFORE the match and does not force the guard down into the arms (the `toml_primary` binding is made above the match and `args.plan` is its fallback), resolve the metrics path by absolutising and canonicalising its longest existing ancestor, the path itself when it exists, and re-appending the components below it (so a log whose leaf does not exist yet still has its directory prefix resolved), and push a problem when the resolved log is not under that root. Where NO plan is read there is no root, so the predicate did not fire and every surface behaved as it did then, which is the answer the no-anchor case above already gets; on `validate --workflow` that case is the match's own `(None, None, _)` arm, already a hard problem for its own reason. A's measured message shape, which reports both paths and the root and tells the user what to do: "`--workflow` would join <source> against <metrics>, which is not under the plan's project root <root>; pass a `--metrics` under that root, or run against the plan's own log". Measured to close both of A's self-found false passes and to resist a `..` escape that climbs out of a fixture root to reach agent-scaffold's own 235-record log. TWO ADJUSTMENTS TO THAT SHAPE FOLLOW FROM THE ROOT DECISION BELOW AND ARE SPECIFIED HERE RATHER THAN MEASURED, because A's build could not tell the two files apart: the first slot names THE PLAN THE CHECK READS, which in A's build was the `--source` and is not always, and the remedy gains a third member for the case where the log was anchored on a different file than the checked plan, "or correct the `--source` and `--plan` pair", since neither of A's two remedies names that cause.

WHY THE ROOT COMES FROM THE CHECKED PLAN AND NOT FROM THE ANCHOR (human, 2026-08-02, receipt `q_id:"Q-55-endproperty"`, ROOT ON THE PLAN THE CHECK READS). The two are not the same file, and the gap between them was MEASURED AT WORK REVIEW on inc1: `resolve_metrics_path` anchors on `--source` first and `--plan` second, while the `--workflow` check reads a TOML-primary `--source` else the Markdown `--plan`, so a Markdown-primary `--source` in one project paired with a `--plan` in another was checked against the FIRST project's log and reported `workflow invariants hold` at exit 0 for a step with no round record of its own. The resolved log is DERIVED from the anchor, so it is always under the anchor's root and a predicate rooted THERE can never fire on that pairing; rooted on the anchor, the END PROPERTY above would have been met by no increment of this step, which is what forced a decision rather than leaving the rooting to the implementer. Three things the implementer should carry. It is ONE predicate and not two conditions layered: is the log I am about to read under the root of the plan I am about to check. In TOML-primary mode the checked plan IS the anchor and the rule is unchanged there; it differs only when a `--source` is given and is not TOML-primary. And it covers the TYPO'D `--source`, a nonexistent `--source` beside a readable `--plan`, where the root comes from the plan that WAS read while the log still comes from the lexical derivation on the path that was not.

BOTH ALTERNATIVES WERE PUT AND REJECTED, so neither is re-opened. A SECOND CONDITION, on the anchor and the checked plan resolving to different roots: rejected as two conditions where one does the work, and because it does not reach the typo'd `--source` at all, since a path that does not exist yields no canonical root and a two-root comparison then has nothing to compare. PARSING THE WHOLE `(source, plan, metrics)` TRIPLE at the boundary into one validated checked-target type: rejected ON SCOPE, NOT ON MERIT. It is the cleaner long-term architecture and would make the divergent pairing UNCONSTRUCTIBLE rather than detected, but it touches the resolution `validate`, `status`, `next` and the ledger path all share, it needs its own risk class and probably its own design pass, and it risks re-opening the already-settled `Q-55-refusalscope` split. If it is ever wanted it belongs in the validation-constraints step beside the queued project-identity work, not here.

WHICH PLAN EACH SURFACE READS IS ALREADY DECIDED IN THE TREE, so the rule names an existing branch rather than adding one. `run_validate`'s `--workflow` match reads the TOML source in its `(Some(source), _, Some(metrics_text))` arm and the Markdown `--plan` in its `(None, Some(plan_text), Some(metrics_text))` arm; `run_status` and `run_next` each project from `toml_source(&args.source)` when that yields a TOML-primary source and fall back to `--plan` otherwise (`src/main.rs:run_status`, `src/main.rs:run_next`), which is the same selection in a different spelling. `status --resume` reads NO plan (`src/main.rs:run_resume` derives `<task>` from the source-or-plan filename and reads only the ledger), so it has no checked plan to root on.

THE LEXICAL/CANONICAL SPLIT IS DELIBERATE AND MUST NOT BE COLLAPSED. The DEFAULT is lexical so the derived path keeps the spelling the caller typed; the GUARD is canonical so it cannot be spoofed by a symlinked source. A built the canonicalising DEFAULT too and measured what it costs: every resolved path becomes absolute even when the user typed a relative source, so two of the three printed lines change on the no-regression case and an absolute machine-specific path lands in output that a pre-commit hook or CI log may be matched against. That is why the fork was resolved this way and not the other; the cost of the split is accepted cost (ii) below.

## One predicate, two responses: the validator refuses, the projections omit (`Q-55-refusalscope`)

`Q-55-mechanism`'s text ("a refusal for unsafe pairings, covering `validate`, `next`, `status` and the ledger path") admitted two readings: the refusal on the validator only, or the refusal on all four surfaces. The second planner pass raised the ambiguity rather than deciding it, and the human decided it with a THIRD option that neither reading contained (receipt `q_id:"Q-55-refusalscope"`, options "Omit the unsafe part, exit 0" / "Narrow: refusal on validate only" / "Wide: refusal on all three", chosen OMIT THE UNSAFE PART, EXIT 0).

THE DECISION. `status` and `next` anchor exactly as the validator does. When the pairing is nonetheless UNSAFE, they OMIT THE WORKFLOW-DERIVED FIELDS, say WHY in their place, and EXIT 0. They neither refuse nor project. The refusal (exit non-zero) remains the validator's alone.

THE GROUND, and it is why this option needs no authorisation against Safe on existing projects while the wide reading would have. `README.md:238` does not merely promise the projections never fail; it says "Unlike `validate` it never fails on a missing or malformed file (a missing part is simply left out of the projection)", and `run_resume`'s doc comment (`src/main.rs`) matches it. A LOG THAT DOES NOT BELONG TO THIS PLAN IS EXACTLY A PART THAT IS NOT AVAILABLE FOR THIS PROJECTION. Omitting it is the documented contract applied LITERALLY, not an exception carved into it. The pass's objection to the wide reading (a hard refusal would break a documented never-fails contract) is therefore resolved rather than overridden, and the projections keep both halves of their contract: they still never fail, and they still leave out what they do not have.

A CORRECTION THE SECOND PASS OWES ON ITS OWN TEXT, because it is what makes this decision necessary rather than decorative. That pass wrote that the anchoring "is what actually removes the fabricated `next` instruction and the leaked resume block". THAT IS TRUE ONLY OF THE DEFAULT `--metrics` CASE. Anchoring changes where the DEFAULT resolves; it does nothing to an EXPLICIT `--metrics` naming a foreign log (explorer A's second false pass, explorer C's attack 4, found independently on different models). Without this decision, `next --source <foreign plan> --metrics <this repository's log>` would keep emitting `state: converged` and `next: mark the step complete` after the whole path fix had landed.

### The exact behaviour, per surface

The trigger is the SAME containment predicate the validator's refusal uses. The predicate is never re-implemented per surface (One source of truth).

- `status`. The metrics half is omitted: print `metrics: unavailable, <reason>` in place of `metrics: <n> records`, where the reason names the resolved log, the derived project root, and that the two do not correspond. The plan half is unaffected and still prints. EXIT 0.
- `status --resume`. Print a note naming the ledger path that was rejected and why, and print NO part of the block. EXIT 0. THIS SURFACE READS NO PLAN, so the rule SUPPLIES a root rather than being re-implemented per surface (`Q-55-resumepairing`, human, 2026-08-02): a `--source` and a `--plan` that both exist must resolve to the SAME root or the block is omitted, and with one alone the anchor is the root, as today. IT IS REACHED BY an explicit `--ledger-fragment` outside that root, and the DEFAULT ledger under a divergent pairing, which the anchoring in inc1 closes only on a single project (measured: `status --resume --source A --plan B` printed A's block at exit 0, and an anchor-rooted inc2 would have kept it).
- `next`. The metrics line is omitted as for `status`, AND the whole `ACTIVE LOOP` block is omitted, AND the `RESUME STATE` echo is omitted when the ledger is the unsafe artifact, with the same note naming the rejected ledger path in its place that `status --resume` prints. In place of the loop, print the existing "no active review loop (`<reason>`)" line with a reason naming the unsafe pairing. THE LEDGER HAS A SECOND WAY TO BE UNSAFE ON `next`, and it follows from the root decision above rather than from a new rule: `default_ledger_path` is anchored `--source` first while the steps come from a TOML-primary `--source` else the Markdown `--plan` (`src/main.rs:run_next`, its `toml_source(&args.source)` branch and the `ledger_fragment ... unwrap_or_else(|| default_ledger_path(...))` beneath it), so a Markdown-primary `--source` in one project beside a `--plan` in another resolves the ledger in the FIRST project while projecting the SECOND project's steps, and echoed one project's `## RESUME STATE` under another's plan on the DEFAULT ledger path. The predicate rooted on the checked plan catches that WHERE THE `--source` LIES OUTSIDE THE CHECKED PLAN'S ROOT; an anchor-rooted one cannot, for the same reason it cannot catch the metrics case, and where it lies INSIDE, neither rooting catches it (the IN-ROOT BOUND below).

`next` MUST NOT EMIT AN ACTION OR A `summary` LINE DERIVED FROM A LOG IT CANNOT VOUCH FOR. This is the specific output the fix must make unreachable, measured by the orchestrator at commit `3170e3f`: `state: converged`, `streak: 1/1`, `rounds: 2/5`, `next: mark the step complete, re-render, and commit`, plus the `summary` line, at exit 0, for a project with ZERO rounds of its own. The block goes as a unit: suppressing only the `next:` line would leave `state`, `streak` and `rounds` standing above it, which is the same foreign evidence in a quieter form. NOT every field of `ActiveLoop` is round-derived, and this argument does not need them to be: `round_cap` comes from the workflow spec, `isolation_tier` is echoed from the CLI, and the `review_findings`/`triage_findings` slots in `context` are built from the task name, as the last bullet of "Scope: what this step does not do" records.

A TRAP THE IMPLEMENTER MUST AVOID, and the reason this is a design constraint rather than a wording preference. The cheap implementation is to treat an unsafe log as an ABSENT one and let the existing code path run. That is wrong and it fabricates in the other direction: `run_next` (`src/main.rs`, the `else` arm of its `metrics_path.exists()` branch) turns an absent log into an EMPTY rounds list and still projects, so a step at `in-progress` with zero visible rounds yields `state: awaiting-first-review` and `next: spawn a reviewer for the first review round`. For a project whose real log says the step converged, that is a fresh false instruction, quieter than "mark the step complete" but still an instruction derived from evidence the tool does not have. UNSAFE IS NOT ABSENT: absent means "this project has no rounds", unsafe means "this tool cannot tell you anything about this project's rounds", and only the second is what the omission must express.

THE PROJECTION SHAPE ALREADY ADMITS THIS, so no new output structure is needed for the human renderer. `NextProjection` (`src/next.rs`) ALREADY CARRIED `metrics: Option<MetricsSummary>`, `active_loop: Option<ActiveLoop>`, `resume_state: Option<String>` and `no_active_loop_reason: Option<String>`, and `render_human` (`src/next.rs`) ALREADY RENDERED the `None` arms. `status`'s `Projection` carries `metrics: Option<MetricsProjection>` the same way. What the change adds is a new REASON reaching those arms, not a new shape, which is the cheaper and safer half of the work (Make illegal states unrepresentable: the state is already representable).

### The machine surface: a serialised reason (`Q-55-jsonreason`)

The second planner pass raised the `--json` surface rather than assuming it, and the human decided it (receipt `q_id:"Q-55-jsonreason"`, options "Add a serialised reason" / "Accept that `--json` reports only absence" / "Defer to the validation-constraints step", chosen ADD A SERIALISED REASON), so a machine consumer can tell an unsafe pairing apart from an absent log and from an absent plan source.

THE PROBLEM, in the form that decided it: THE OMIT HALF OF `Q-55-refusalscope` WAS MET ON BOTH SURFACES AND THE SAY WHY HALF WAS MET ONLY ON ONE. `no_active_loop_reason` WAS `#[serde(skip)]` (`src/next.rs:NextProjection::no_active_loop_reason`) and `status`'s `Projection` HAD no reason field at all, so under `--json` an omitted part serialised as a bare `null` with nothing distinguishing why. THE REASONING THE HUMAN ACCEPTED, recorded so this is not read as scope creep: `--json` is the surface AGENTS consume, and this whole decision exists because an agent ACTS on `next`'s output. Letting the human renderer explain itself while the machine surface reports a bare absence INVERTS the reasoning that produced `Q-55-refusalscope` in the first place. It also leaves a machine consumer arguably worse off than before the omit landed, since `active_loop: null` is equally readable as "nothing to do".

THIS IS A DOCUMENTED-CONTRACT CHANGE AND IS TREATED AS ONE. Four doc claims were falsified or made incomplete by it, found by sweeping `src/next.rs` and the `status` projection for exhaustiveness claims rather than by patching the one already known.

- `src/next.rs:NextProjection::no_active_loop_reason`'s doc comment BECAME FALSE and had to change: "Why there is no active loop, for the human renderer. Not serialised (the JSON contract is exactly the fields above)". Both halves go: the field is no longer human-renderer-only, and the contract is no longer exactly the fields above.
- `NextProjection`'s own doc comment (`src/next.rs`) BECAME INCOMPLETE: "Every derived part is optional so a missing plan or log yields a partial projection rather than a failure (mirrors `status`'s `Projection`)". It enumerated the causes of an absent part as a missing plan or a missing log, and an unsafe pairing is neither; the enumeration is precisely what this change exists to make reportable, so leaving it two-thirds complete is the defect in miniature.
- `status`'s `Projection` doc comment (`src/main.rs:Projection`) HAD THE SAME DEFECT: "Every part is optional so a missing plan or metrics file yields a partial projection rather than a failure".
