Note the two are tied by the cross-reference in `NextProjection`'s own doc comment (`src/next.rs`, "mirrors `status`'s `Projection`"), so fixing one and not the other leaves a claim of correspondence asserting away a real difference. Both change or neither does.
- `resume_state`'s doc comment (`src/next.rs:NextProjection::resume_state`) WAS SHORT BY ONE IN THE SAME WAY: "or `None` when the ledger is absent or carries no such section" names two causes, and an unsafe `--ledger-fragment` is a third.

A FIFTH ITEM FOUND BY THE SWEEP IS PRE-EXISTING AND IS NOT A CONSEQUENCE OF THIS CHANGE, recorded because the enum makes it checkable. `active_loop`'s doc comment (`src/next.rs:NextProjection::active_loop`) SAID it was `None` when "all steps complete, every pending step blocked, or no plan source", while `select_active_loop` (`src/next.rs`) returns `Some(build_pending_loop(step, LoopState::Blocked, blockers, spec, context))` from its last branch for a pending step with unmet blockers, so that case yields an ACTIVE LOOP and is not a cause of `None` at all. The enum's variant set must match WHAT THE CODE CAN ACTUALLY DISTINGUISH. Do NOT add a blocked-steps variant to satisfy the comment; that would be new behaviour, and the comment was the thing that was wrong.

WHAT THE SWEEP FOUND NOTHING OF, stated because a negative result is worth recording. No `skip_serializing_if` appears in either `src/next.rs` or `src/main.rs`, and the new field must follow that convention: ALWAYS PRESENT, `null` in the normal case. No other doc comment in either file claims its JSON output is exhaustive.

A CONSEQUENCE THE IMPLEMENTER SHOULD MEET DELIBERATELY RATHER THAN BY SURPRISE, AND IT IS GOOD NEWS. `next`'s JSON is pinned by a byte-compare golden, `GOLDEN_JSON` (`src/next.rs:tests::GOLDEN_JSON`) asserted by `golden_json` (`src/next.rs:tests::golden_json`), so adding a field BREAKS THAT TEST and the contract change cannot land silently: the golden diff is the reviewable artifact for it. The human text is pinned the same way by `GOLDEN_HUMAN` and `golden_human_text`. THE ASYMMETRY MATTERS THOUGH: `status --json` has NO golden, and HAD no test on its serialisation at all (its only path is the `serde_json::to_string_pretty` call in `src/main.rs:run_status`), so the `status` half of this change WAS UNGUARDED and a mistake there FAILED nothing. That is why the acceptance check runs the binary against `status --json` explicitly rather than relying on the suite.

### The field shape and the value vocabulary

Specified here rather than left to the implementer, because the entire point is that a consumer can TELL THE CAUSES APART, and an under-specified vocabulary would reproduce the defect in a new place. Closed enums, not free strings (Make illegal states unrepresentable), serialised kebab-case, following the in-file precedent of `LoopState` (`src/next.rs`, `#[derive(..., Serialize)]` plus `#[serde(rename_all = "kebab-case")]`, which is what puts `awaiting-reviewers` on the wire in the golden today). THE ENUM IS THE MACHINE VALUE ONLY: the paths a human message names are not carried on it, so the CALLER assembles that message from the paths it already holds, which is what lets a unit variant serialise as a bare token while the human text still names the log and the root.

`metrics_absent_reason`, on BOTH `NextProjection` and `status`'s `Projection`, beside the existing `metrics` field. `Some` exactly when `metrics` is `None`. This reason and `resume_state_absent_reason` below are computed by the CALLER and passed through `NextInputs` alongside `metrics_records` and `resume_state`, so `project` stays a pure function of its inputs.

- `log-absent`: no file found at the resolved metrics path.
- `log-not-this-project`: the resolved path is not under the root, so the tool cannot vouch that its records belong to that plan. This is the `Q-55-refusalscope` case.

`no_active_loop_reason`, on `NextProjection`, RETYPED from `Option<String>` to a closed enum and NO LONGER `#[serde(skip)]`. Retyping is preferred over adding a parallel serialised field: one reason, one type, rendered two ways, rather than two representations of the same fact that can disagree (One source of truth). The human renderer maps each existing variant back to the exact string it prints today, so `render_human` output and its golden are unchanged and the retype is behaviour-preserving on the human surface. `no_loop_reason`'s third string, "no in-progress or ready step", WAS UNREACHABLE for the reason given above and the reconciliation collapsed it to two answers, so no variant is specified for it.

- `no-plan-steps`, printed as today's "no plan steps found".
- `all-steps-terminal`, printed as today's "all steps complete".
- `metrics-not-this-project`, the NEW case: the round log resolved for this plan is not the plan's own, so no loop state can be derived from it. Printed with a reason naming the resolved log and the derived root.

`resume_state_absent_reason`, on `NextProjection`, beside `resume_state`. `Some` exactly when `resume_state` is `None`. This one is included rather than skipped because without it the same defect lands on a third field: after inc2, `next --json` can omit the resume block for a THIRD reason and report the same bare `null` it reports for the other two. Two of the three causes WERE already distinguished IN THE CODE at `src/main.rs:run_next`, where `ledger_path.exists()` being false and `extract_resume_state` returning `None` WERE separate branches that both COLLAPSED to `None`, so naming them COST nothing beyond the naming.

- `ledger-absent`: no file found at the resolved ledger path.
- `no-resume-section`: the ledger exists but carries no `## RESUME STATE` block.
- `ledger-not-this-project`: the resolved ledger is not under the root, which is either an explicit `--ledger-fragment` outside it or, on `next`, a DEFAULT ledger anchored on a `--source` that itself lies outside it. Both members are CONTAINMENT and neither is a project-identity test: a `--source` in a different project reaches this only when that project is not NESTED inside the root.

THE PRECEDENCE RULE, on both path fields: where an absent cause and an unsafe cause both apply, THE UNSAFE VARIANT WINS, because unsafe is not absent (above) and a bare absence is exactly the conflation this vocabulary exists to prevent.

THE CORRELATION RULE, so a consumer can join the fields rather than guess. On an unsafe metrics pairing, `metrics_absent_reason` is `log-not-this-project`, and `no_active_loop_reason` is `metrics-not-this-project` WHEN the loop's absence is metrics-derived rather than step-derived. The shared `not-this-project` token is deliberate: it is the same cause reported as two consequences, and a consumer that recognises the token needs no lookup table to correlate them.

WHAT HAS NO JSON SURFACE AT ALL, so nothing is owed there and no acceptance check demands it: `status --resume` returns from `run_resume` at `src/main.rs:run_status`'s `return run_resume(&args)` early return, BEFORE any serialisation, so `--resume` is human text only and `--json` alongside it is silently ignored today. The implementer must not invent a JSON reason for that path. That the flag is silently ignored is a pre-existing oddity of a shape this project elsewhere constrains in clap (`--ledger-fragment` carries a `requires` for exactly this stated reason at `src/main.rs:StatusArgs::ledger_fragment`, and `audit --out` carries a `conflicts_with = "json"` at `src/main.rs:AuditArgs::out` for the mutually-exclusive-output-modes case this one actually is); it is NOT caused by this step, it was raised rather than folded in, and it is now scheduled as its own backlog step, `status-resume-ignores-json` (order 96).

WHAT WAS CONSIDERED AND DELIBERATELY NOT ADDED. A reason beside `status`'s `plan: Option<PlanProjection>`: that field has exactly ONE cause (no readable plan source was given), so a reason field there would carry a single value and inform nobody (Minimal by default). A malformed-log variant on `metrics_absent_reason`: neither `status` nor `next` distinguishes a malformed log today (`count_records` counts non-blank lines and `parse_rounds` is best-effort), so there is no such state to report, and manufacturing one would be new behaviour rather than a reason for existing behaviour.

## Candidate (d) is rejected, with the evidence, so it is not revisited

The first planner pass named a `[meta]`-declared log path as "where the cleaner long-term architecture points". Explorer B BUILT it, including the sibling and ledger extensions, and argued against it; explorer C reached the same vulnerability independently. It is rejected on measured grounds, recorded here so the direction is closed rather than rediscovered.

- IT CONTRIBUTES NOTHING ON THE DAY IT SHIPS. B ran the borrowed-slug fixture under both absent-field policies against ONE build with a BYTE-IDENTICAL plan file. Holding the absent-field case at the CWD default left the false pass reproducing unchanged; anchoring it killed the false pass. Every line of the difference is candidate (a). The field is absent from this repository's plan and from the scaffolded template (measured at zero occurrences in both), so 100 percent of (d)'s effect comes from the changed default.
- IT IS A NEW WAY TO WRITE THE DEFECT DOWN PERMANENTLY. A plan declaring `metrics = "../../../../docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl"` reconstructs the full false pass, and the reconstruction is WORSE in three measured respects: it is CWD-INDEPENDENT (it reproduces from inside the fixture, where the defect did not fire at all), it is COMMITTED to a tracked file so it reproduces on every machine and in CI, and it passes `validate --source` clean so nothing warns.
- THE VALIDATOR CANNOT REFUSE IT. The conventional log lives OUTSIDE the plan directory (`docs/plans` to `docs/metrics`), so the source-relative spelling of the DEFAULT itself needs a `..` component, which is the exact component `is_safe_sidecar_ref` (`src/plan/source.rs:480-495`) exists to forbid. The project's existing containment rule is unusable for this field, and the strongest rule available, "not absolute", stops nothing. That is a LAYOUT fact, not an implementation choice. C reached the same conclusion as its attack 3 and cited the same in-repo precedent unprompted.
- IT COVERS LESS THAN (a) DOES. A Markdown plan has no `[meta]` to declare anything in, so the `--plan` substrate is entirely untouched by (d). B re-rendered a fixture so its Markdown Roadmap genuinely carried the borrowed slug at `complete` and reproduced the full false pass against its own FIXED build via `validate --plan`. Candidate (a) derives its root from the `--source` OR the `--plan` path, so one rule covers both substrates. On coverage, (a) is the more complete mechanism and (d) is the partial one, which points the opposite way from the first pass's framing of (a) as the cheap fix and (d) as the principled one.
- CORRECTION TO THE FIRST PASS'S COST LIST FOR (d). It listed "a schema field, its validation, its render, and a migration story". THE RENDER COST IS ZERO: `render` reads only `meta.title` (`src/plan/render.rs:296`) and `meta.sidecars` (`:167-169`), and B ran `render --check` against this repository's own plan WITH the field declared and got "up to date", then restored the plan and confirmed an empty `git diff --stat docs/`. The real cost is one the first pass did not name: `Meta` carries `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` (`src/plan/source.rs:102`), so the field is a HARD PLAN-FORMAT VERSION FENCE, and a plan that declares it is `malformed` to any binary predating it, with no version negotiation in the schema to soften it. This bullet is relevant only as the record of why the first pass's cost accounting should not be reused; (d) is rejected on the four grounds above, not on its cost.

ONE NARROW THING FROM B'S BUILD IS WORTH RECORDING AND IS NOT SHIPPED: `[meta].ledger`, not `[meta].metrics`, is the field where a declaration would be defensible, because the ledger sits BESIDE the plan so its source-relative default is a bare filename with no `..`, which means `is_safe_sidecar_ref` CAN be applied to it unchanged. That is the opposite of the priority (d) implies. It is not built here: a declaration would add a capability nobody has asked for (Minimal by default).

## The four accepted costs

Each was measured, each was put to the human, and each was ACCEPTED, (i) and (ii) as part of `Q-55-noconvention`, (iii) as `Q-55-conventionlesscost` and (iv) as `Q-55-resumecost`. The ledger records the first as "THE ACCEPTED COST, which the implementer must not treat as an oversight to fix". They are recorded here for two audiences: an implementer must NOT "fix" them, and a reviewer must NOT raise them as defects. The acceptance check below PINS all four as expected behaviour, because a check that pins an accepted cost is worth more than a note asking people to remember it.

(i) A BARE FILENAME RUN FROM INSIDE `docs/plans` WAS A SILENT MISS. `cd <root>/docs/plans && agent-scaffold validate --source p.plan.toml --workflow` derives the root from a source path with no parents to walk, falls back to the source's own directory, and looks for `docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl` beneath it, which does not exist. The project's real log is never read. This is NOT a regression (the pre-fix build was identically wrong here), and the containment guard STRUCTURALLY CANNOT catch it, because the wrong path is still inside the right project: containment is not correctness. The canonicalising default variant does fix it, at the output-stability cost described above, which is why it was not taken. After the tier policy landed, this case became a HARD FAILURE naming the path it looked for rather than a silent green, which is arguably the right outcome anyway and is the form the acceptance check pins.

(ii) A SYMLINK ON THE PLAN'S OR THE LOG'S PATH BECOMES A FALSE POSITIVE ON THE PREDICATE. Where `<root>/docs/plans` is a symlink to `<root>/elsewhere`, the canonicalised plan and the canonicalised log land under different roots, and the guard wins: A measured this layout going from reading its 37-record log to `exit=1 REFUSED`. THE COST IS THE DIVERGENCE AND NOT THE LAYOUT: any symlink that makes the canonicalised checked plan and the canonicalised resolved log fall under different roots produces it, on either side, and `docs/plans` is the placement that was MEASURED rather than the population. This is a genuine new failure for a layout that worked before inc2, and it is the main false-positive risk in the mechanism. The judgement taken, and it is a judgement rather than a measurement: a loud refusal beats a silent wrong file (Fail loudly), and the canonicalising variant that would remove the divergence turns every printed metrics path absolute, changing output on the correct case. There is a related backlog step in the same family, `sidecar-ref-symlink` (order 64, `deferred`), which is where a symlink-aware treatment belongs if one is ever wanted; it is NOT this step's job. AFTER `Q-55-refusalscope` THIS COST HAS TWO MANIFESTATIONS AND ONLY ONE OF THEM IS LOUD: on `validate --workflow` the layout gets a refusal that names itself, while on `status` and `next` it gets a quiet OMISSION, so a user of that layout sees the projections stop reporting round evidence they legitimately have. The acceptance check pins both manifestations, and a reviewer should read the quiet one as the more expensive half of an accepted cost, not as a separate defect.

(iii) A SAME-PROJECT `--plan` OUTSIDE ANY `docs/plans`, WITH A MARKDOWN-PRIMARY `--source` INSIDE ONE, IS REFUSED (`Q-55-conventionlesscost`, human, 2026-08-02). `--source <root>/docs/plans/x.plan.toml --plan <root>/notes/p.md` greened before inc2 against `<root>/docs/metrics/workflow.jsonl`; after inc2 the checked plan's root is `<root>/notes`, through `src/main.rs:project_root_of_source`'s fallback to the checked plan's own directory, and the log is not under it, so `--workflow` exits non-zero and `status` and `next` omit their metrics half. CARVING THE CASE OUT WAS DECLINED because it would REVERSE `Q-55-noconvention`, which decided the containment refusal is layered ON TOP of that fallback rather than suppressed by it.

(iv) `status --resume` ON THE SAME PAIR OMITS THE PROJECT'S OWN BLOCK, in EITHER `primary` spelling, so its population is WIDER than (iii)'s.

A FURTHER BEHAVIOUR CHANGE IS NOT A COST BUT SHOULD BE STATED: any setup that deliberately points one project's `--metrics` at a log outside its own root now exits 1 under `--workflow`. The end property `Q-55` requires demands this, but it is a break for anyone doing it on purpose, and the CHANGELOG entry must say so.

## What this step does not fix, and where it goes instead

THE IN-ROOT BOUND. CONTAINMENT REFUSES ONLY WHAT LIES OUTSIDE THE CHECKED PLAN'S ROOT SUBTREE, so every foreign artifact inside that subtree is invisible to it: a log copied to this plan's own `docs/metrics/`, and equally a NESTED project's own log and ledger at their own conventional paths, the log then joining by bare slug. A measured the copied case by copying agent-scaffold's 235-record log into a fixture's own `docs/metrics/` and watching `workflow invariants hold` at exit 0 for a project with no review evidence: the guard passes (the log IS under the fixture's root), and W3 joins `triager-runs-only-on-findings` by bare slug against a record belonging to another project. Neither the anchor nor the refusal touches this. Both are PATH fixes; the DATA MODEL is untouched, and W3 still joins on a bare slug (`src/workflow.rs:448-449`).

PROJECT IDENTITY IS QUEUED TO THE VALIDATION-CONSTRAINTS STEP AND IS NOT BUILT HERE (`Q-55-mechanism`). This is now a working proof rather than a prediction: explorer C BUILT it, as an optional `project: Option<String>` on `Round` (`src/metrics.rs`) and on `[meta]` (`src/plan/source.rs`), with `check_workflow_toml` pre-filtering the rounds when the plan declares an id, treating a round with no `project` field as "not this project" so the change is a strict tightening rather than a new loophole. C measured it as the ONLY mechanism that separates two projects LEGITIMATELY SHARING ONE MERGED LOG, which no path mechanism can address, and as a no-op when undeclared. C also reported its own limitations unprompted, and the queued step inherits all three: it is OPT-IN, so an unmigrated plan is unprotected and `scaffold` would need to mint an id for it to protect new projects by default; the minimal-diff filter placement does NOT cover `next`, which derives its forward convergence verdict independently rather than through `w3_problems` (`src/next.rs:has_risk_class_conflict`'s doc comment), so a filter placed inside `run_checks` leaves it unprotected; and `decisions` and `escalations` are read unfiltered, so W4 and W5 keep their bare-slug exposure. B's negative result belongs to the same queued step and should be carried into it: declaring the log's LOCATION does not establish that the log BELONGS to the plan, and building a path field first would make the identity work harder, because the identity check would then have to reconcile itself against a declared path that may disagree with it. THE QUEUED STEP OWNS THE LOG HALF OF THE IN-ROOT BOUND ONLY: filtering `Round` records cannot change which ledger file `src/main.rs:run_next` opens, so the LEDGER half of that bound has NO OWNER in this plan today, recorded here rather than scheduled.

COSTS (iii) AND (iv) SHARE ONE ROOT CAUSE, `src/main.rs:project_root_of_source`'s fallback to the plan's own parent, and treating it ONCE IS QUEUED TO THE SAME STEP rather than accumulating a fresh accepted cost on every new surface. That fallback is not REQUIRED for the in-root bound.

## The increments, and why in this order

`Q-55-scope` (human, 2026-07-31, receipt `q_id:"Q-55-scope"`) decided ONE STEP with SEPARATE INCREMENTS, over a separate step ahead of `Q-55` and over folding this into the validation-constraints step, on the reasoning that the defects touch the same code path and produce the same user-facing green, so separate steps would mean reviewing the same region twice while separate increments keep each change reviewable on its own terms. That decision named TWO increments, because the step was then TWO defects. The count is now UNDER-SPECIFIED rather than wrong: what the human decided is the DIVISION PRINCIPLE, and the set below is that principle re-applied to the widened scope, not an appendix to the old pair.

The division follows one rule: an increment is a unit whose review asks ONE question. Where two pieces of work would be reviewed by asking the same question, they are one increment; where they would be reviewed by asking different questions, they are separate.

- `workflow-enforcement-tier-inc1`, THE RESOLUTION RULE AND ALL OF ITS CALL SITES. `--metrics` becomes `Option<PathBuf>` on `ValidateArgs`, `StatusArgs` and `NextArgs`; the lexical nearest-wins derivation and the metrics resolution land; `validate`, `status` and `next` all use them; `default_ledger_path` takes the plan source and resolves the ledger BESIDE it, with both call sites (`run_resume` and `run_next`) passing it through. Plus the help strings and doc comments that describe resolution, and the red-then-green tests. NO new REFUSAL mechanism: any new non-zero exit comes from the pre-existing W3 check finally running against the right project, which is check 4's whole point. With BOTH a `--source` and a `--plan`, the anchor follows the source-then-plan order `derive_task` already uses (`src/next.rs`); with NEITHER, the ledger keeps today's `docs/plans/<task>.ledger.md`, as the metrics rule keeps its CWD-relative path for the same case. The review question is "does the derivation name the right file, in every layout".
- `workflow-enforcement-tier-inc2`, THE CONTAINMENT PREDICATE AND ITS CONSUMERS. The canonical root derivation FROM THE PLAN EACH SURFACE READS (`Q-55-endproperty`, which is what makes the predicate reach a divergent `--source`/`--plan` pairing), the resolve-as-far-as-possible resolution, the predicate itself, and then the responses `Q-55-refusalscope` settled: `validate --workflow` REFUSES (a problem, exit non-zero), `status` and `next` OMIT the affected parts with a reason at exit 0, and `status --resume` omits the block. Plus the serialised reasons `Q-55-jsonreason` settled, so the omission explains itself on `--json` as well as in the human text, with the four falsified doc comments corrected in the same change. Plus the `--workflow` help enumeration, the README notes for the new error, the new omitted part and the new JSON fields, the CHANGELOG entry, and its own red-then-green tests. The review question is "does the predicate identify an unsafe pairing correctly, and does each consumer give the right answer to it, on both surfaces".
- `workflow-enforcement-tier-inc3`, THE TIER POLICY AND THE `SE-3` DOCUMENTATION HALF. The `_` catch-all of `src/main.rs:run_validate`'s `--workflow` match becomes a reported problem so `--workflow` exits non-zero, plain `validate` untouched; the `run_validate` doc comment corrected; `pack/AGENTS.md:93` qualified and the two deployed copies regenerated; the README `validate` paragraph and the CHANGELOG entry. Plus its own red-then-green test. The review question is "is the two-tier boundary now both enforced and truthfully described".
- `workflow-enforcement-tier-inc4`, THE DOCUMENTATION-CURRENCY PASS THAT CLOSES THE STEP, and the only increment here that ships no behaviour. This file's own descriptions of `src/main.rs`, `src/next.rs`, the test suite, `README.md` and `pack/AGENTS.md`, which the three increments above falsified as they landed, re-tensed to the pre-increment state they were written about or deleted where the sentence carried nothing else; the acceptance-check preamble's stale count of the red-then-green demonstrations inc2 owes, deleted rather than corrected; acceptance check 16, widened to pin the probe that cannot answer beside the log that is absent; the citation drift this step's own line-number movement caused in the sidecars of `test-tmpdir-repo-assumption` (order 95), `checks-runner-worktree-name-collision` (order 93) and `instrument-magic-filename` (order 60); `Projection.plan`'s false doc comment at `src/main.rs:Projection` (`Q-55-plandoccurrency`); and this description. The review question is "does every claim this step leaves behind match the tree it leaves behind".

WHY THE FOUR CALL SITES ARE ONE INCREMENT AND NOT TWO OR THREE. They share one function. Splitting `validate`'s anchoring from the siblings' would review the same derivation twice, which is exactly what `Q-55-scope` rejected at the step level, and it would leave the tree in a state where two commands disagree about which log belongs to a plan, an inconsistency neither endpoint has and one that an implementer and a reviewer would each have to reason about. The ledger's finding that the projections are "arguably the MORE urgent half" points the same way: deferring them to a later increment is the wrong direction. The ledger path is a genuinely DIFFERENT rule (the source's own directory, no upward walk, no fallback) and a different defect class (content injection rather than a wrong count), but it is roughly ten lines; giving ten lines their own convergence loop is disproportionate (Minimal by default). It stays in inc1, and this paragraph exists so a reviewer does not expect the upward walk there and flag its absence.

WHY THE PREDICATE IS ITS OWN INCREMENT. It carries a known false positive (accepted cost (ii)); and it deliberately uses a DIFFERENT resolution from the default, so its review must check the lexical/canonical SPLIT rather than one rule. Its correctness property is also a negative ("must never pair..."), which the design pass showed is not established by passing the obvious tests: the anchor passed the first pass's own reproduction while leaving two further false passes standing.

WHY THE OMIT BEHAVIOUR LANDS IN INC2 AND NOT IN INC1, WHICH IS NOT WHERE IT FIRST LOOKS LIKE IT BELONGS. It is the projections' own behaviour, not the containment refusal, so inc1 is the natural first guess. The derivation forces inc2, for two reasons. FIRST, the omit is TRIGGERED BY THE CONTAINMENT PREDICATE and by nothing cheaper: no lexical test separates an explicit `--metrics` naming a foreign log from an explicit `--metrics` naming the plan's own log spelled differently; A's guard exists because the lexical comparison gets the symlink case wrong. Putting the omit in inc1 therefore means putting the PREDICATE in inc1, which drags inc2's hardest review question (a negative property, established only by adversarial construction) forward into an increment whose question is a positive one, and leaves inc2 as a bool turned into a `problems.push`. SECOND, the responses are only reviewable AGAINST EACH OTHER. The whole content of `Q-55-refusalscope` is that one predicate yields DIFFERENT answers on the validator and on the projections, so the defect to catch is a consumer wired to the wrong response, which is invisible unless they are read side by side. The same applies to accepted cost (ii): the symlinked-`docs/plans` false positive now has TWO manifestations, a loud false refusal in `validate` and a QUIET FALSE OMISSION in `status` and `next`, and those are not equally acceptable (a false omission in a surface an agent consumes withholds true evidence without saying anything is wrong with the tool), so the judgement has to be made over both at once or it is not made at all.

WHY THE SERIALISED REASONS LAND IN INC2 TOO, derived rather than assumed. The tempting framing is that this is the same predicate yielding a THIRD response, which would put it in inc2 by the argument above. That framing is wrong and the right one is stronger: the JSON reason is not a third response, it is the SECOND RENDERING of one response. The predicate yields two responses (refuse, omit), and the omit has two renderings (human text, JSON). Splitting the renderings across increments would mean inc2 COMPUTES a reason, prints it to text, and discards it for JSON, and a later increment re-surfaces a value that already existed, which is a deliberate half-done state across a boundary bought for nothing. Worse, it would ship a NEW behaviour with its explanation missing on exactly the surface the behaviour exists for: `Q-55-refusalscope` is about output an agent acts on, and an agent reads `--json`. That is a different and weaker position than the inc1-to-inc2 gap, which leaves an EXISTING defect open for one increment rather than shipping a new silence. Two mechanical reasons agree: the enums are consumed by the same code that computes the omission, and `status --json` has no golden test, so separating the JSON work would land the unguarded half of it with no co-located human-renderer behaviour to check it against and would force the acceptance check to rebuild the unsafe fixture a second time. One fixture answers both surfaces if they land together.

THE COST OF THAT PLACEMENT, STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN. After inc1 alone, `next --source <foreign plan> --metrics <this repository's log>` STILL emits `state: converged` and `next: mark the step complete`. That is a known defect deliberately left open across an increment boundary, exactly as inc1 alone leaves defect A open by design, and it is the reason inc2 is not optional polish: inc2 closes the agent-facing half of defect C, which the design pass judged the more urgent half. An implementer must not read inc1's acceptance checks as evidence that defect C is closed.

WHY THE DOCUMENTATION HALF SHIPS WITH THE TIER POLICY AND NOT SEPARATELY. The pack sentence's truth is a FUNCTION of the tier policy's behaviour, so reviewing the sentence requires running the tier policy's cases; separating them would make the second reviewer redo the first reviewer's runs. More importantly, the interval between them is not neutral: as set out under defect D, a tier policy without its qualifier leaves a non-instrumented user hitting a hard error from a check the guidance still promises them unconditionally, which is worse than the gap either change leaves alone. The mechanism documentation for inc1 and inc2 (help strings, the README anchoring note, the doc comments) travels with ITS increment for the same currency reason, and there is deliberately NO separate documentation increment for the SHIPPED prose: this project already carries a step about documentation currency, and shipping behaviour with stale prose beside it is the defect that step exists to remove. THIS FILE'S OWN CLAIMS ABOUT THE TREE ARE THE ONE EXCEPTION, and they are inc4; the Documentation impact section states why that exception is measured rather than preferred.

THE ORDER IS inc1 -> inc2 -> inc3 -> inc4, AND EVERY EDGE IS LOAD-BEARING. INC4'S EDGE IS THE CHEAPEST TO STATE AND WAS MEASURED RATHER THAN ARGUED: inc1's own review converted a set of `src/main.rs` citations, and inc2 and inc3 falsified them again, so a currency pass that runs while the code is still moving is provably wasted work. It runs when the code stops moving, which is after inc3 and before the step goes `complete`. The first planner pass argued that the path fix must precede the tier policy, because a user whose `--workflow` run started failing could "fix" it by running from a directory that happens to contain a log, which is exactly the contaminated green of defect B, so the tier policy would hand users a workaround into the worse bug. THAT ARGUMENT STILL BINDS, and the design pass GENERALISES it: the tier policy goes LAST because EVERY escape hatch a user reaches for is closed by an earlier increment. Standing somewhere else is closed by inc1. Passing `--metrics` by hand at a foreign log is closed by inc2, and it is not hypothetical: it is explorer A's second false pass and explorer C's attack 4, found independently on different models. Landing the tier policy before either would convert a quiet defect into a loud prompt to reach for the two workarounds that are still open. Inc1 precedes inc2 because the guard reuses inc1's root derivation, and because a guard without an anchor is candidate (b) standing alone, which refuses every cross-directory run until the user passes `--metrics` by hand, the objection the first pass correctly raised against (b) as an alternative.

## Risk classification

Each increment is argued on its own evidence. The first pass's "both risky" is NOT inherited; of the three arguments that pass could have reached, two are new here and the third has gained a factor it did not have.

`workflow-enforcement-tier-inc1` is RISKY (two consecutive clean rounds). It changes WHICH FILE the tool reads on every invocation of THREE commands that do not pass `--metrics`, plus which LEDGER two of them read, and the failure mode of a wrong anchor is not a crash but a confident wrong answer. The design pass measured that this failure mode IS SELF-CONCEALING: A's own build, correct on the reported reproduction, was still emitting `workflow invariants hold` at exit 0 on two other inputs until A attacked it deliberately, and nothing in the output distinguished the correct runs from the wrong ones. That is the same class of defect the increment exists to remove. It also COMPOUNDS FORWARD: after inc3 a mis-derived anchor stops being "reads the wrong file" and becomes "hard-fails a correctly instrumented project", so an inc1 defect escalates into a broken gate rather than staying a quiet one. The derivation additionally makes at least one SILENT JUDGEMENT CALL that no measurement settled (nearest-wins on a nested `docs/plans`), which is precisely the kind of thing a review round exists to catch. Relative-path handling is this tree's recorded weak spot rather than a neutral area: `is_safe_sidecar_ref` (`src/plan/source.rs:480-495`) exists because of it, and two backlog steps sit in the same family (`sidecar-ref-empty-string` order 63, `sidecar-ref-symlink` order 64). The counter-argument, that the eventual diff is small (A measured the anchor at `+79/-15`, mostly comments) and that there is a deterministic test for it, loses to the blast radius: every future invocation of the project's main validation surface, plus the agent-facing `next`, whose wrong answer is an instruction rather than a report.

`workflow-enforcement-tier-inc2` is RISKY (two consecutive clean rounds), and for reasons that do not overlap inc1's. It INTRODUCES a non-zero exit on validator invocations that succeeded before inc2 AND withholds output from projection invocations that answered before inc2, and it does so with a MEASURED FALSE POSITIVE already in hand (accepted cost (ii), the symlinked `docs/plans` directory), so it is a deliberate, knowing break of Safe on existing projects rather than a strict tightening. Its correctness property is a NEGATIVE, and the design pass demonstrated that a build satisfying the stated reproduction can still admit the defect class by two other routes, so passing the increment's own tests is explicitly NOT sufficient evidence here; the review has to include adversarial construction, which is what a second clean round buys. It is also the only place in the mechanism where TWO DIFFERENT RESOLUTIONS (lexical default, canonical guard) run against each other by design, and the disagreement between them is simultaneously the source of the guard's strength (it cannot be spoofed by a symlinked source) and of its one false positive, so a reviewer who checks only one of the two has not checked the mechanism. `Q-55-endproperty` SHARPENS THAT RATHER THAN ADDING A CLASS: the two resolutions can now start from DIFFERENT FILES, the log from the `--source`-first anchor and the root from the plan the check reads, so rooting the guard on the anchor is a defect that check 11 passes over. `Q-55-refusalscope` ADDS A FACTOR RATHER THAN LEAVING THE CLASS UNCHANGED: one predicate now drives responses, two of which must NOT fail, so the failure this increment can ship is not only "refuses the wrong thing" but "refuses on a surface that must never refuse" or "omits on a surface that should have refused", and its false positive is now partly SILENT, since a false omission in `next` withholds true evidence from an agent without signalling that anything went wrong. `Q-55-jsonreason` adds a second: the increment now also changes a DOCUMENTED JSON CONTRACT on two commands, falsifying four doc comments and breaking a byte-compare golden. None of this changes the class, since the increment was already `risky`, but it widens what the two rounds have to cover and a reviewer who checks only `next --json` has checked the guarded half. The counter-argument, that it is roughly 80 lines sharing inc1's derivation, is about diff size and not about blast radius, which this project has already recorded losing.

`workflow-enforcement-tier-inc3` is RISKY (two consecutive clean rounds). It changes a CLI EXIT CODE, the most externally depended-on contract the tool has, and it is INTENDED to flip a currently-passing gate to failing for every non-instrumented project, which is exactly the population Safe on existing projects protects. That principle is not overridden lightly; what authorises the break is Structured data first, project for humans, whose own text records the human's 2026-07-18 decision that at this pre-adoption stage the best long-term design wins over backwards-compatibility and that it beats Safe on existing projects where the two conflict. AN AUTHORISED BREAK IS A REASON TO MAKE THE CHANGE, NOT A REASON TO REVIEW IT LESS. The boundary is easy to get subtly wrong in a way tests may not catch by accident: the `_` catch-all of `src/main.rs:run_validate`'s `--workflow` match covers BOTH the TOML-source-present and the Markdown-plan-present variants of "metrics missing", and the fix must convert exactly those to problems without capturing a case that should stay a skip and without touching the no-`--workflow` path at all. THE FACTOR THE FIRST PASS DID NOT HAVE: this increment now also edits the SHIPPED PACK and regenerates two DRIFT-GUARDED deployed files, and its pack content is a COVERAGE CLAIM about an enforcement boundary. That is the one artifact species this project has calibration data on, and the data is bad: step 92 spent six rounds and fifteen findings on one such claim, all of them prose, zero mechanism defects, joint-third of the artifacts ever reviewed against a project median of two rounds, with the ledger's own diagnosis being that "a coverage claim is unusually easy to falsify at an edge". The counter-argument, that the in-tree precedent of that match's `(None, None, _)` arm (`src/main.rs:run_validate`) makes the code half a three-line change, is true and does not reach the other half.

`workflow-enforcement-tier-inc4` is RISKY (two consecutive clean rounds), classified at loop-open so the required count is a PROPERTY OF THE ARTIFACT rather than a fresh judgement each round, which is what the convergence rule demands. The artifact is a DOCUMENTATION-CLAIM SURFACE, and that is this project's measured worst review class on its own calibration data. Step 92 (`prompt-drift-guard`) spent SIX rounds and FIFTEEN valid findings on ONE coverage claim, all of them prose and none of them a mechanism defect. Inc1 OF THIS VERY STEP spent THREE rounds and 13 valid findings, EVERY ONE an inaccurate description of correct behaviour and zero defects in what the code does. The counter-argument, that a documentation pass changes no behaviour so one clean round is enough, is the precise reasoning that produced both of those loops, so it is recorded here as REJECTED rather than left for a reviewer to re-derive. Two factors are specific to this increment and neither is present in inc1 to inc3. FIRST, ITS FAILURE MODE IS THE ONE IT EXISTS TO REMOVE: a pass that re-tenses a false claim can write a NEW false claim in its place, and this project has five retrospective and one prospective measurement that a fix pass which AUTHORS prose manufactures the next round's finding while a deletion-class pass re-seeds nothing, so a reviewer must check what was written and not only what was removed. SECOND, ITS EVIDENCE IS MECHANICAL AND CHEAP TO PRODUCE, which cuts the other way: every claim here is a citation or a quotation, so a round that reads prose without opening the cited range has not reviewed it, and the acceptance check below is stated so that the round report can show the ranges rather than assert the conclusion.

## Acceptance check

Every claim below is a command with an expected exit code, so a round is settled by running it rather than by reading the diff. `Q-66` (reproducible evidence proportional to the claim, step `reviewer-reproducible-evidence`, order 88) applies: all four defects are behavioural, so EACH INCREMENT THAT CHANGES BEHAVIOUR owes at least one test that is RED against the pre-fix build and green after, and the round report must state WHICH MUTATION or WHICH PRE-FIX REVISION produced the red. The red case for inc1 is the borrowed-slug false pass at check 4; for inc2 they are the explicit-relative-`--metrics` false pass at check 11 (the validator's response), the divergent `--source`/`--plan` pairing at check 13b (the same response on the case an anchor-rooted predicate cannot reach, `Q-55-endproperty`, and the one that decides whether this increment closes the end property), the fabricated `next` instruction at check 14b (the projections' response in human text), and the absent reason fields at check 14e (the same response on the machine surface, where the red is that the fields do not exist at all before the change), each owed because one predicate with several consumers on two surfaces is not evidenced by testing one consumer on one surface; for inc3 it is the exit code at check 15. THAT ENUMERATION IS A FLOOR AND NOT A TOTAL, and no total is stated here on purpose: every fix round that closes a defect owes its own red-then-green beside these, so a stated count goes stale inside the loop it describes.

BEFORE RUNNING ANY OF THIS: point `TMPDIR` at a directory OUTSIDE any git repository. Three of the suite's tests (`checks::tests::a_non_repo_target_with_runnable_checks_errors`, `tests::init_plan_defaults_to_git_and_skips_inside_a_repo`, `tests::install_precommit_hook_skips_a_non_repo`) build a scratch directory under `std::env::temp_dir()` and assert it is NOT inside a repository, so a worktree-internal `TMPDIR` fails them spuriously. All three explorers hit this and all three correctly isolated it as unrelated to their changes. It is a property of the suite, not of this step; it is held by its own backlog step, `test-tmpdir-repo-assumption` (order 95), and this step does not fix it.

1. Build: `cargo build`. Suite and lint: `cargo test` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, both clean. Plan render pinned: `cargo run -- render docs/plans/agent-scaffold.plan.toml --check`.
2. Rebuild the fixture from scratch (the command at the top of this file) and confirm `docs/metrics/` is absent: `ls "$SCRATCH/docs"` prints only `plans`.
3. AFTER INC1, defect B's original reproduction is dead: from the agent-scaffold root, `agent-scaffold validate --source "$SCRATCH/docs/plans/TEMPLATE.plan.toml" --workflow` does NOT read agent-scaffold's own log and does NOT print `workflow invariants hold`. ## Documentation impact

All in-repo. Each item below travels with the increment that makes it stale, WITH ONE EXCEPTION: the claims THIS FILE makes about the tree, which are collected in inc4 and land last. THE EXCEPTION IS MEASURED RATHER THAN PREFERRED. Inc1's own review converted a set of `src/main.rs` citations, and inc2 and inc3 then falsified them again, which is why inc1 was waived on the explicit ground that its residual defects were claims a later increment would falsify a second time. A currency pass on this file run before the code stops moving therefore does work it will have to redo, so it is scheduled once and at the end. It is a documentation step OWED, and naming it as one is the honest form: the alternative was to keep converting the same citations three times.

### `test-tmpdir-repo-assumption`: three tests read the ambient repository state through `TMPDIR`, so following this project's own scratch-`TMPDIR` discipline makes a correct tree fail

A suite defect, not a product defect. Three tests require the directory `std::env::temp_dir()` returns to be OUTSIDE any git repository. `temp_dir()` honours `TMPDIR`, and this project instructs every spawned agent to point `TMPDIR` at a scratch directory, which agents naturally place inside their worktree, which is a git repository. The three tests then fail on a tree with nothing wrong with it.

This is a FALSE RED, which is the mirror of the false-green family most of this plan is about, and its cost is the same shape one step removed: a suite that fails for reasons unrelated to the change under test teaches its readers to classify failures as spurious, and that habit is how a real failure eventually gets waved through. It also costs agent time directly, measured below.

Scheduled as backlog behind the release gates. It blocks nothing and nothing blocks it; it is deliberately NOT a dependency of `rename-to-agent-flow` or of `workflow-enforcement-tier`. Scheduled by human decision (2026-07-31) against the standing backlog, with no `[[question]]` registered and no decision receipt owed, on the precedent of the 2026-07-30 release-gated resequencing.

## The three tests, and why each assertion is reasonable in itself

None of the three is wrong about the product. Each pins a real behaviour, and the behaviour it pins is one this project deliberately has.

- `checks::tests::a_non_repo_target_with_runnable_checks_errors` (`src/checks.rs:1477-1486`). Asserts `run(&dir, Isolation::WorkingTree)` returns `Err(RunError::NotARepo(_))`. Reasonable: `checks` runs its lint and format commands inside a throwaway git worktree so an in-place formatter can never mutate the live tree, and a target that is not a repository has no worktree to make, so erroring rather than silently running in place is the whole safety property.
- `tests::init_plan_defaults_to_git_and_skips_inside_a_repo` (`src/main.rs:2289-2305`). Its FIRST assertion is the ambient-dependent one: `init_plan(Vcs::Git, &root)` must be `InitPlan::Init` in a fresh non-repo directory. The later assertions (a directory with a `.git`, and a subdirectory of one, both give `SkipExists`) construct their own condition and are unaffected. Reasonable: scaffolding into a populated repo must never re-initialise it (Safe on existing projects), and the `Init` case is the other half of that pair; without it the test would pass while `init_plan` skipped unconditionally.
- `tests::install_precommit_hook_skips_a_non_repo` (`src/main.rs:2878-2889`). Asserts `install_precommit_hook(&root)` returns `HookInstall::Skipped(reason)` with the reason containing "not a git repository". Reasonable: the hook install is create-if-absent and must degrade to a noted skip rather than failing the scaffold, and this is the case that pins the note.

Observed failures, verbatim, from an explorer running with `TMPDIR` inside its worktree:

```
---- checks::tests::a_non_repo_target_with_runnable_checks_errors stdout ----
expected NotARepo, got Ok(Report { results: [CheckResult { name: "ok", kind: Lint, status: Passed }], config_present: true })
---- tests::init_plan_defaults_to_git_and_skips_inside_a_repo stdout ----
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: SkipExists
 right: Init
---- tests::install_precommit_hook_skips_a_non_repo stdout ----
assertion failed: reason.contains("not a git repository")
test result: FAILED. 370 passed; 3 failed
```

## The mechanism

Two separate scratch helpers, both rooted at the ambient temp directory:

- `src/checks.rs:1037-1046`, `fn scratch(name)`, builds `std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("agent-scaffold-checks-test-{pid}-{name}"))`.
- `src/main.rs:2279-2287`, a second `fn scratch(name)`, builds `std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("agent-scaffold-poc-{pid}-{name}"))`.

`std::env::temp_dir()` honours `TMPDIR` on Unix. The three tests then exercise code whose repository detection walks UP from the given directory, so a `TMPDIR` anywhere inside a worktree, including a linked worktree, resolves to a directory that IS inside a repository and the not-a-repo precondition silently does not hold. Nothing in the tests states the precondition, so the failure presents as a product assertion failing rather than as an environment mismatch, which is why every agent that hits it spends time deciding whether it broke something.

Note the contrast already present in the same file: `checks::tests::an_empty_repo_with_no_commits_errors` (`src/checks.rs:1488-1498`) calls `init_repo(&dir)` to CONSTRUCT the git condition it needs rather than inheriting it. The suite therefore already has the pattern for the positive case; only the negative case was left to ambient state.

## The evidence, and the tension that is the actual defect

Not hypothetical. On 2026-07-31 the metrics-path design pass dispatched three worktree-isolated explorers, each briefed per the project's own discipline to point `TMPDIR` at a scratch directory inside its worktree. ALL THREE HIT THIS, all three correctly isolated it as unrelated to their changes, and all three reported it unprompted; one routed around it by using the session scratchpad, outside any repository, for `cargo test` while keeping the worktree-local directory for build artefacts and fixtures. No result was corrupted, and the cost was three agents' time on a trap the brief set. The ledger records it as an orchestrator defect with the cure "brief a scratch `TMPDIR` OUTSIDE any git repository", and adds that "the collision is also a real property of the suite and is now recorded as such".

THE TENSION IS THE DEFECT, and it is why the cure alone is not the fix. The scratch-`TMPDIR` discipline exists for a measured reason: an earlier reviewer left 32272 directories in `/tmp`, and the standing rule that followed is to brief every agent to use a scratch `TMPDIR` and report its `/tmp` count. So the project has two disciplines that contradict each other on the same variable: use a scoped scratch `TMPDIR` so agents cannot litter, and do not put `TMPDIR` anywhere the suite can see a repository. Every agent briefed for this repository has to be told about the collision by hand, which is a rule that lives in prose and gets forgotten rather than in the thing that enforces it. Removing the tension means the suite stops depending on where `TMPDIR` points at all.

## Fix options, not pre-decided

The implementer picks one and argues it in the commit, or raises the choice if it reads as a genuine fork. Both are viable and they trade differently.

- (A) MAKE THE PRECONDITION DETERMINISTIC rather than ambient. Have the three tests construct a directory that is provably outside any repository instead of assuming one, for example by asserting the precondition explicitly and failing with an environment message when it does not hold, or by giving git an explicit boundary (`GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES`, or a `.git` sentinel arrangement) so the upward walk stops before it leaves the scratch directory. Keeps all three assertions intact and has the in-file precedent noted above (the positive case already constructs its condition). The risk to watch is that a boundary applied carelessly makes the not-a-repo condition hold BY CONSTRUCTION in a way that would also hold if the product stopped detecting repositories at all, which turns a real test into a vacuous one.
- (B) CHANGE WHAT THE TESTS ASSERT, dropping or weakening the not-a-repo cases. Cheapest, and wrong on current reading: each assertion pins a real safety property (do not run checks outside a worktree, do not re-initialise an existing repo, do not fail the scaffold over an uninstallable hook), so weakening them buys suite determinism by deleting coverage. Recorded so the option is visibly considered and visibly rejected rather than silently unconsidered.
- (C) LEAVE THE TESTS AND FIX THE BRIEF, that is, make the scratch-`TMPDIR` rule say "outside any repository" everywhere it appears. This is what is being done today by hand. It is not a fix: it keeps a suite whose result depends on an environment variable, and it relies on prose that every future brief must remember, which is precisely the class of rule this project keeps finding drifts.

Recommendation: (A), with (B) rejected on coverage and (C) rejected as a workaround already in force. State which of (A)'s two routes was taken and why.

## Risk classification

`test-tmpdir-repo-assumption-inc1` is `low_risk` (one clean review round). The change is confined to `#[cfg(test)]` code in two files, touches no product behaviour, ships nothing to a scaffolded project, and is reversible in a single revert. It differs in kind from the other test-isolation step in this plan, `checks-runner-worktree-name-collision` (order 93, `risky`), which changes how `src/checks.rs` NAMES worktrees and so touches production code.

The one failure mode that would justify a second round is a test made to pass by construction rather than by the property holding, which is the false-green shape this project cares most about, appearing inside the suite itself. It is foreclosed cheaply rather than by an extra round: `Q-66` already requires evidence proportional to the claim, and the proportionate evidence here is a MUTATION DEMONSTRATION, breaking each of the three product behaviours in turn and showing the corresponding test goes RED under the new arrangement. A round report that shows three reds and three greens has answered the only question the classification turns on, and a second clean round would add nothing to it. If the implementer cannot produce those three reds, the classification was wrong and the step should be re-classified before it converges rather than waived afterwards.

## Acceptance check

1. `cargo test` passes with `TMPDIR` set INSIDE a git repository (a worktree-local scratch directory), which is the case that fails today.
2. `cargo test` still passes with `TMPDIR` set OUTSIDE any repository, and with `TMPDIR` unset, so the fix removes the dependency rather than inverting it.
3. `cargo test` passes with `TMPDIR` set inside a LINKED worktree specifically, not only inside a primary checkout, since that is the arrangement every isolated agent on this project actually runs in.
4. The mutation demonstration, one per test, each producing a named RED against the new arrangement: make `run` accept a non-repository target, make `init_plan` skip unconditionally, and make `install_precommit_hook` report something other than the not-a-repository skip. Each corresponding test must fail. The round report names the mutation and quotes the failure.
5. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean.
6. No production behaviour changed: the diff touches only `#[cfg(test)]` code, or, if it does not, the step is re-classified before converging.
7. Neither scratch helper leaves directories behind: check the `/tmp` (or `TMPDIR`) entry count before and after a full run and report it, which is the discipline whose collision with the suite this step exists to remove.

## Scope

- It does not change `src/checks.rs`'s worktree NAMING, which is the separate defect held by `checks-runner-worktree-name-collision` (order 93). The two are both test-isolation defects and are deliberately separate: that one is a real race in production-reachable code, this one is an environment assumption in test setup.
- It does not consolidate the two `scratch` helpers into one. They live in different modules and differ in their prefix and their cleanup, and merging them is a refactor this defect does not require (Minimal by default). If the chosen fix makes a shared helper natural, say so and argue it rather than doing it silently.
- It does not change the project's scratch-`TMPDIR` discipline or any agent brief. Those stay as they are; what changes is that following them stops breaking the suite.

### `status-resume-ignores-json`: `status --resume --json` silently ignores `--json` and prints human text

A small consistency defect on the CLI surface, found while specifying the JSON reasons for `workflow-enforcement-tier` (`Q-55-jsonreason`) and deliberately not folded into that step. `run_status` dispatches to the resume slice before any serialisation happens, so `--json` passed alongside `--resume` has no effect at all: no JSON, no warning, no non-zero exit.

Scheduled as backlog behind the release gates by human decision (2026-07-31), against the standing backlog, with no `[[question]]` registered and no decision receipt owed, on the same precedent as `test-tmpdir-repo-assumption` (order 95). It blocks nothing and nothing blocks it; it is deliberately NOT a dependency of `rename-to-agent-flow`, of `workflow-enforcement-tier`, or of `test-tmpdir-repo-assumption`.

## The mechanism

`run_status` (`src/main.rs`) opens with the resume branch and returns from it:

```rust
fn run_status(args: StatusArgs) -> io::Result<()> {
	// The thin `status --resume` slice: print the ledger's `## RESUME STATE` block
	// verbatim (reusing the same extractor `next` uses) instead of the state projection.
	// A missing ledger, an absent section, or a ledger that is not this plan's is a note and
	// exit 0, not a failure (`status` is best-effort).
	if args.resume {
		return run_resume(&args);
	}
```

Every serialisation path in `status` is BELOW that return: the projection is assembled afterwards and `serde_json::to_string_pretty` is reached in `run_status`'s `if args.json` branch (`src/main.rs`). `run_resume` (`src/main.rs`) only ever `println!`s. So `args.json` is read nowhere on the resume path, and clap accepts the pair without complaint.

## The observed behaviour, run rather than reasoned

Four cases, all against a build of this worktree, with a two-line probe ledger outside the repository.

A, the resume block present. `--json` has no effect; the raw Markdown block is printed:

```
$ agent-scaffold status --source docs/plans/agent-scaffold.plan.toml --resume --json --ledger-fragment <probe>.ledger.md
## RESUME STATE

probe ledger body.
exit: 0
```

B, the ledger absent:

```
no ledger at <path>; nothing to resume
exit: 0
```

C, a ledger with no `## RESUME STATE` section:

```
<path>: no `## RESUME STATE` block found
exit: 0
```

D, THE CONTROL, which is what makes this a dispatch problem rather than a broken flag. Without `--resume`, the same `--json` works exactly as documented:

```
$ agent-scaffold status --source docs/plans/agent-scaffold.plan.toml --json
{
  "plan": {
    "steps": [
...
```

So the flag is fine and is simply never reached. In all three resume cases the output is not JSON and the exit code is 0.

## Severity, stated honestly so the queue is not distorted

THIS IS A FALSE SILENCE, NOT A FALSE ASSERTION, and it is milder than anything `workflow-enforcement-tier` fixes. It must not borrow that step's urgency just because it was found next to it.

The caller asked for JSON and got output that is visibly not JSON, so any consumer that parses it fails on the first character, immediately and locally. Nothing wrong is propagated: there is no wrong value, no fabricated instruction, and no green that should have been red. Compare the defects that step exists to fix, where the tool emits a CONFIDENT WRONG ANSWER that a human or an agent then acts on. Here the tool emits a right answer in the wrong format, and the format mismatch is self-announcing.

What the defect actually costs is DIAGNOSIS, not correctness. The failure surfaces to the user as "the tool produced garbage" rather than as "you passed a flag that does nothing here", so the user debugs their parser before they suspect their command line. That is a real cost and a small one.

## The in-repo precedent, which makes this an inconsistency rather than a gap

This project has already ruled on silently-ignored flags, in this file, with the reasoning written down. `StatusArgs` itself carries one, on `StatusArgs::ledger_fragment` (`src/main.rs`), the sibling flag of the very branch in question:

```
/// ... Requires --resume (the flag is meaningless without it, and would otherwise be silently ignored on an exit-0 run).
#[arg(long, requires = "resume")]
ledger_fragment: Option<PathBuf>,
```

"the flag is meaningless without it, and would otherwise be silently ignored on an exit-0 run" is exactly the condition `--json` is in under `--resume`, on the same struct, one field away. The same sentence appears again on `--workflow-spec` (`src/main.rs:ValidateArgs::workflow_spec`, "the flag is meaningless without it, and would otherwise leave a malformed spec unparsed and exit 0"), and a third, shorter form on `render --strict` (`src/main.rs:RenderArgs::strict`, "Meaningless without --check").

There is also a precedent for the RELATION this case needs, which is not the same relation as those three. `audit` resolves a clash between two mutually exclusive OUTPUT MODES at `src/main.rs:AuditArgs::out`:

```
/// Override the report output path. ... Conflicts with --json, which writes no file.
#[arg(long, conflicts_with = "json")]
out: Option<PathBuf>,
```

So a fix here FOLLOWS AN ESTABLISHED CONVENTION rather than inventing one, and that is the proposition to state in the commit. Five constraint attributes already exist in `src/main.rs` (`ScaffoldArgs::dry_run`, `ValidateArgs::workflow_spec`, `StatusArgs::ledger_fragment`, `RenderArgs::strict`, `AuditArgs::out`), so the mechanism is routine in this codebase.

## The fix fork, not pre-decided

- (A) REJECT THE COMBINATION WITH A CLAP CONSTRAINT. `--resume` and `--json` are two mutually exclusive OUTPUT MODES, so the relation is `conflicts_with`, matching the `audit --out` precedent, NOT `requires`, which is the relation the other three precedents use. Getting that backwards matters: a `requires` in either direction would break `status --json` on its own, which is a working, documented surface with a README example. Cost is one attribute, one help-text sentence on each flag, and a test per direction. Promises nothing new, closes the defect exactly as stated, and is a one-attribute revert if the project later wants (B).
- (B) GIVE `--resume` A REAL JSON SURFACE. Serialise the resume block and its absence reason instead of rejecting the pair. Materially larger, and it answers a DIFFERENT question, namely whether `status --resume` should have a machine surface at all, which nobody has asked for. IT MUST NOT BE BUILT BEFORE `workflow-enforcement-tier` INC2 LANDS. That increment introduces `resume_state_absent_reason` on `NextProjection` with the closed vocabulary `ledger-absent` / `no-resume-section` / `ledger-not-this-project`, and those are the same three causes a resume JSON surface would have to report. Building (B) first would mint a second vocabulary for one set of causes, which is the "an under-specified vocabulary reproduces the defect in a new place" hazard in a new place, and it would then have to be reconciled. If (B) is ever chosen, it REUSES that enum.

RECOMMENDATION: (A). It closes the defect at the size of the defect (Minimal by default), it follows two in-file conventions rather than inventing one, and it forecloses nothing, since (A) and (B) are mutually exclusive in the long run and (A) is trivially revertible if appetite for (B) appears. (B) is a capability question wearing a defect's clothes.

NOTE ON WHY THE (B) ORDERING IS NOT ENCODED IN `blocked_by`. It is conditional on a fork nobody has chosen, and under the recommended (A) this step is not blocked by anything. Encoding a dependency for a branch that may never be taken would make the step falsely blocked and would drag it into `workflow-enforcement-tier`'s wake, which is the opposite of what scheduling it as independent backlog was for. The constraint is stated here in prose instead; an empty `blocked_by` is deliberate, not an oversight.

## Risk classification

`status-resume-ignores-json-inc1` is `low_risk` (one clean review round), AS SCOPED TO FORK (A).

The change is one clap attribute plus help text and tests. It touches no logic, changes no output for any invocation that is not currently meaningless, ships nothing to a scaffolded project, and reverts in one line. It DOES turn a currently-accepted invocation into a usage error (exit 2), which is a CLI contract change, and this plan classifies `workflow-enforcement-tier-inc3` as `risky` partly on that basis; the two are not comparable. Inc3 flips a currently-PASSING gate to failing for an entire population, on an invocation people run in CI, and its boundary (which cases convert to problems and which stay skips) is easy to get subtly wrong. Here the rejected combination has never done what its flags advertise, so nothing can be depending on the behaviour being removed; the break is loud, immediate, names both flags, and is fixed by deleting one of them.

The one real way to get this wrong is naming the WRONG RELATION or putting the attribute on the wrong field, which would break `status --json` standing alone, a documented surface with a README example. That is a single-attribute mistake with a single-test detection, which is what one clean round with a mandated control case is for; a second round would re-read one attribute.

IF FORK (B) IS CHOSEN INSTEAD, THIS CLASSIFICATION DOES NOT HOLD and the step must be RE-CLASSIFIED BEFORE IT IS BUILT rather than waived afterwards. (B) adds a serialised contract, must reuse another step's vocabulary, and would carry the same documented-contract obligations `Q-55-jsonreason` carries (doc comments, `README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`).

## Acceptance check

1. `cargo test` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean. Point `TMPDIR` outside any git repository first, per `test-tmpdir-repo-assumption` (order 95).
2. THE DEFECT IS CLOSED: `agent-scaffold status --source <plan> --resume --json` exits NON-ZERO with a usage error naming both flags, rather than exit 0 with human text. Red against the pre-fix build, where it exits 0 printing the `## RESUME STATE` block.
3. THE CONTROL, which is the mistake this step can actually ship and must be pinned in BOTH directions: `status --source <plan> --json` alone still emits the projection as JSON and exits 0, and `status --source <plan> --resume` alone still prints the block and exits 0. A fix that spells the relation backwards passes check 2 and fails one of these.
4. The two remaining resume paths are unchanged when `--json` is absent: a missing ledger prints `no ledger at <path>; nothing to resume` at exit 0, and a ledger with no section prints `<path>: no ``## RESUME STATE`` block found` at exit 0.
5. `--ledger-fragment` still requires `--resume` and is unaffected, so the new constraint did not disturb the existing one on the same struct.
6. `--help` for `status` reads correctly with the new constraint, and the help text on each flag states the exclusion in the style the five existing constraint attributes use.

## Scope

- It does not give `status --resume` a JSON surface. That is fork (B), it is not recommended, and it must not be built before `workflow-enforcement-tier` inc2 in any case.
- It does not audit the other subcommands for silently-ignored flag combinations. Five constraint attributes already exist and the three cases they cover are the ones previously found; a sweep for further cases is a different piece of work and is not smuggled in here (Minimal by default). If the implementer notices one while working, RAISE it rather than folding it in.
- It does not change `run_resume`'s output, its exit code, or its best-effort contract.

### `validation-constraints`: state W5's waiver-ownership rule against the round log so the two owed waivers become writable (`Q-70`), then treat the validator-cluster defects, the `agent-scaffold next` defects, project identity and the detection mechanisms the record routes here

One thing in this step blocks another step today and the rest of it does not. W5's increment-ownership rule decides whether a `[[step.waiver]]` may name a given increment by a LEXICAL STRIP of the increment's own id (`leading_slug(increment) != waiver.step`, `src/workflow.rs:564`), while W3 decides which step an increment belongs to STRUCTURALLY, from the round log (`round_step_slug` at `src/workflow.rs:119` and `round_increment_id` at `:127`). Where the two disagree, no waiver can be written at all. Two are owed on `workflow-enforcement-tier`, which cannot go `complete` until they can be written.

PROVENANCE. `Q-55-entryroute` (2026-08-11, receipt record 308) scoped a design pass to the validator cluster, meaning the W5 fix plus the three detection mechanisms, over three alternatives one of which was splitting the W5 fix into its own minimal step.
